lessons.title: Gaseous Exchange in Plants
lessons.notes_html:
What is gaseous exchange?

Gaseous exchange means the exchange of gases like oxygen and carbon dioxide between an organism and the environment. This exchange takes place in two life processes: in photosynthesis as well as in respiration.

How do plants exchange gases?

Plants carry out gaseous exchange through the root, the stomata and the stem; all these parts take part in gaseous exchange.

  • Leaves: mainly take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen through the stomata.
  • Stem: exchanges gases through lenticels.
  • Root: the root also exchanges gases.

Stomata and guard cells

A stoma is a small pore in a leaf. Each stoma is surrounded by two guard cells. The guard cells help in opening and closing the stoma.

Why are stomata open during the daytime?

During the day carbon dioxide is needed for photosynthesis, so the stomata stay open so that carbon dioxide can enter and oxygen can leave.

Other organisms and the body surface

Some organisms exchange gases through the whole body surface without special organs, e.g. the earthworm, the frog (through its skin), and single-celled organisms like Amoeba.

Experiment: carbon dioxide in respiration

Germinating seeds are placed in a flask and the air passing from it is passed through lime water → the lime water turns milky → this proves that carbon dioxide is released during respiration.

options: The breakdown of food in cells to release energy
The exchange of gases like oxygen and carbon dioxide between an organism and the environment
The movement of air in and out of the lungs only
The opening and closing of pores in a leaf
mcqs.q: What does gaseous exchange mean?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the exchange of gases like oxygen and carbon dioxide between an organism and the environment. The notes define gaseous exchange in exactly this way. It is a swapping of gases with the surroundings, not the breakdown of food inside cells.

options: Only in respiration
Only in photosynthesis
In photosynthesis as well as in respiration
In digestion and in excretion
mcqs.q: In which two life processes does gaseous exchange take place?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is in photosynthesis as well as in respiration. The notes state that this exchange takes place in both of these life processes. So gaseous exchange is not linked to only one process.

options: The root, the stomata and the stem — all of these
Only through the stomata
Only through the root
Only through the stem
mcqs.q: Through which parts do plants carry out gaseous exchange?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the root, the stomata and the stem, because the notes say all these parts take part in gaseous exchange in plants. No single part alone is the full answer. Each of the three parts plays its own role.

options: They take in oxygen and release carbon dioxide through lenticels
They release carbon dioxide only through the root
They stop all gas exchange during the day
They take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen through the stomata
mcqs.q: What do leaves mainly do during gaseous exchange?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that leaves take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen through the stomata. The notes describe this as the main gas movement in leaves. The stem, not the leaf, is the part that uses lenticels.

options: Through stomata
Through lenticels
Through guard cells
Through lime water
mcqs.q: Through which structures does the stem exchange gases?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is lenticels, because the notes state that the stem exchanges gases through lenticels. Stomata and guard cells belong to the leaf. This keeps the role of each plant part separate and clear.

options: A small pore in a leaf
A large opening in the stem
A cell that traps dust in the nose
A flask used for germinating seeds
mcqs.q: What is a stoma?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is a small pore in a leaf. The notes define a stoma in exactly these words. Each such pore is surrounded by guard cells that control it.

options: One guard cell
Four guard cells
Two guard cells
Three guard cells
mcqs.q: Each stoma is surrounded by how many guard cells?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is two guard cells, because the notes say each stoma is surrounded by two guard cells. These two cells help in opening and closing the stoma. No other number is given in the notes for a stoma.

options: They turn lime water milky
They carry out photosynthesis alone
They trap dust and germs from the air
They help in opening and closing the stoma
mcqs.q: What is the function of the guard cells?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that guard cells help in opening and closing the stoma. The notes give this as their role around each pore in the leaf. Trapping dust and germs is done by hairs and mucus in the nose, not by guard cells.

options: Because carbon dioxide is needed for photosynthesis, so carbon dioxide can enter and oxygen can leave
Because the plant needs to release carbon dioxide for respiration only
Because guard cells cannot close in sunlight
Because oxygen is needed for photosynthesis in the leaves
mcqs.q: Why do stomata stay open during the daytime?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that during the day carbon dioxide is needed for photosynthesis, so the stomata stay open for carbon dioxide to enter and oxygen to leave. The notes link the daytime opening directly to photosynthesis. This is why the pores do not stay closed in the day.

options: That oxygen is released during respiration
That carbon dioxide is released during respiration
That oxygen is taken in during photosynthesis
That carbon dioxide is absorbed by the seeds
mcqs.q: In the experiment with germinating seeds, what does lime water turning milky prove?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that carbon dioxide is released during respiration. In the experiment, air from the flask of germinating seeds is passed through lime water and the lime water turns milky. The notes state that this result proves carbon dioxide is given out during respiration.

lessons.title: Gaseous Exchange in Humans: Pathway and Lungs
lessons.notes_html:
The human respiratory pathway

In humans the pathway of air is in this order:

Nose → pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli

Air enters through the nose, passes through the pharynx and larynx into the trachea, then through the bronchi and bronchioles to the alveoli, where gaseous exchange takes place.

Why is breathing through the nose better?

The nose has hairs and mucus which trap dust and germs and clean the air, and warm and moisten it; the mouth does not provide this protection, so breathing through the nose is better than breathing through the mouth.

Where is the larynx?

The larynx is present at the start of the trachea. It comes after the pharynx and before the trachea in the pathway.

Respiratory surface and alveoli

The respiratory surface in humans is the alveoli, i.e. the air sacs. Real gaseous exchange takes place at the surface of the alveoli, not in the nose, trachea or bronchioles — those are only the pathway.

Features of a good respiratory surface

  • It should be thin and moist.
  • It should be permeable, i.e. gases can pass through it easily.
  • It should be very large, so that more gas can be exchanged.

When all these features are present together, the exchange is fast and efficient.

options: Nose → trachea → pharynx → larynx → alveoli → bronchi → bronchioles
Nose → pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli
Nose → larynx → pharynx → bronchioles → trachea → bronchi → alveoli
Nose → pharynx → trachea → larynx → bronchioles → bronchi → alveoli
mcqs.q: What is the correct order of the human respiratory pathway?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is nose, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles and then alveoli. The notes give the pathway of air in exactly this order. Air finally reaches the alveoli, where gaseous exchange takes place.

options: In the nose
In the trachea
At the alveoli
In the bronchioles
mcqs.q: Where does gaseous exchange actually take place in humans?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is at the alveoli, because the notes say air travels through the pathway to the alveoli, where gaseous exchange takes place. The nose, trachea and bronchioles are only parts of the pathway. Real exchange happens only at the alveoli.

options: The nose has hairs and mucus which trap dust and germs and clean, warm and moisten the air
The nose connects directly to the alveoli
The mouth lets carbon dioxide enter the blood
The nose makes the chest capacity increase
mcqs.q: Why is breathing through the nose better than breathing through the mouth?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that the nose has hairs and mucus which trap dust and germs and clean the air, and warm and moisten it. The notes add that the mouth does not provide this protection. That is why breathing through the nose is better.

options: At the end of the bronchi
Inside the alveoli
Between the bronchioles and the alveoli
At the start of the trachea, after the pharynx and before the trachea
mcqs.q: Where is the larynx present?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is at the start of the trachea, coming after the pharynx and before the trachea in the pathway. The notes fix the position of the larynx in exactly this way. It is not located near the bronchi or the alveoli.

options: The alveoli, i.e. the air sacs
The surface of the nose
The surface of the trachea
The surface of the pharynx
mcqs.q: What is the respiratory surface in humans?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the alveoli, which the notes also call the air sacs. Real gaseous exchange takes place at the surface of the alveoli. The other parts named are only the pathway that carries air to them.

options: It should be thick and dry
It should be thin and moist
It should be very small in size
It should not let gases pass through it
mcqs.q: Which feature must a good respiratory surface have?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that a good respiratory surface should be thin and moist. The notes list this as one of its required features. A thick and dry surface would not allow fast and efficient exchange.

options: It should trap dust and germs
It should be covered with hairs and mucus
Gases can pass through it easily
It should open and close like a pore
mcqs.q: What does it mean that a respiratory surface should be permeable?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that gases can pass through it easily, because the notes explain permeable in exactly these words. Permeability is one of the features of a good respiratory surface. It has nothing to do with hairs, mucus or pores.

options: So that air can be warmed and moistened
So that the pathway becomes longer
So that dust can be trapped in it
So that more gas can be exchanged
mcqs.q: Why should a respiratory surface be very large?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is so that more gas can be exchanged, as stated directly in the notes. A very large surface gives more area for exchange to happen. Together with being thin, moist and permeable, this makes exchange fast and efficient.

options: The exchange is fast and efficient
The exchange becomes slow and weak
Gases stop passing through the surface
Air stays only in the nose and trachea
mcqs.q: What happens when all the features of a good respiratory surface are present together?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that the exchange is fast and efficient. The notes say this happens when the surface is thin and moist, permeable and very large all together. Missing any of these features would reduce how well gases are exchanged.

options: Real gaseous exchange takes place in all of them
They are only the pathway, and real exchange takes place at the alveoli
They are the respiratory surface in humans
They are air sacs where oxygen enters the blood
mcqs.q: Which statement about the nose, trachea and bronchioles is correct?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that the nose, trachea and bronchioles are only the pathway, while real gaseous exchange takes place at the surface of the alveoli. The notes make this distinction clearly. Calling these parts the respiratory surface would therefore be wrong.

lessons.title: The Process of Breathing
lessons.notes_html:
Difference between three terms

TermMeaning
Breathing (ventilation)Movement of air in and out
Gaseous exchangeSwapping of gases between the body and the environment
RespirationChemical process in cells in which food is broken down to release energy

Breathing in — inspiration

  • The intercostal muscles contract.
  • The diaphragm contracts.
  • The ribs move outward and upward, not inward.
  • The chest capacity increases and air rushes in.

Order: muscles contract → chest capacity increases → air rushes in

Breathing out — expiration

In exhalation (expiration) the muscles relax, the chest capacity decreases and air is pushed out.

Inhaled and exhaled air

AirOxygenCarbon dioxide
InhaledMoreLess
ExhaledLessMore, and it is warm and moist

Why does the breathing rate rise?

A rise in carbon dioxide in the blood increases the breathing rate. During or after exercise breathing also becomes faster, because the muscles need more energy, which needs more oxygen and produces more carbon dioxide to be removed.

Oxygen debt

During hard exercise the muscles work without enough oxygen and lactic acid is formed; the extra oxygen needed afterwards to remove that lactic acid is called oxygen debt.

options: A chemical process in cells that releases energy
The swapping of gases between the body and the environment
The movement of air in and out
The removal of lactic acid from muscles
mcqs.q: What is breathing, also called ventilation?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the movement of air in and out, because the notes define breathing or ventilation in exactly this way. It is different from gaseous exchange and from respiration. Keeping these three terms separate is the point of the lesson.

options: The movement of air in and out of the chest
A chemical process in cells in which food is broken down to release energy
The swapping of gases with the environment
The contraction of the diaphragm and ribs
mcqs.q: What is respiration?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is a chemical process in cells in which food is broken down to release energy. The notes define respiration in this way, unlike breathing which is only air movement. Respiration happens inside cells, not in the chest pathway.

options: The intercostal muscles contract, the diaphragm contracts, the ribs move outward and upward, chest capacity increases and air rushes in
The muscles relax, chest capacity decreases and air is pushed out
The ribs move inward and the diaphragm relaxes
Carbon dioxide is broken down in cells to release energy
mcqs.q: What happens during breathing in, or inspiration?
mcqs.why: The correct answer describes inspiration: the intercostal muscles and diaphragm contract, the ribs move outward and upward, chest capacity increases and air rushes in. The notes also stress that the ribs do not move inward at this stage. Relaxing muscles and pushing air out belong to expiration instead.

options: Air rushes in → chest capacity increases → muscles contract
Chest capacity increases → muscles contract → air rushes in
Muscles relax → air rushes in → chest capacity increases
Muscles contract → chest capacity increases → air rushes in
mcqs.q: What is the correct order of events in inspiration?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is muscles contract, then chest capacity increases, then air rushes in. The notes give this exact sequence for breathing in. Air cannot rush in before the chest space has first become larger.

options: The diaphragm contracts and the ribs move upward
The muscles relax, the chest capacity decreases and air is pushed out
The chest capacity increases and air rushes in
The intercostal muscles contract strongly
mcqs.q: What happens during breathing out, or expiration?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that in expiration the muscles relax, the chest capacity decreases and air is pushed out. The notes describe exhalation in exactly this way. Contraction of muscles and an increase in chest capacity happen during inspiration, not expiration.

options: Inhaled air has less oxygen and more carbon dioxide than exhaled air
Both have exactly the same amounts of oxygen and carbon dioxide
Inhaled air has more oxygen and less carbon dioxide; exhaled air has less oxygen and more carbon dioxide
Exhaled air has more oxygen and less carbon dioxide than inhaled air
mcqs.q: How do inhaled and exhaled air differ in oxygen and carbon dioxide?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that inhaled air has more oxygen and less carbon dioxide, while exhaled air has less oxygen and more carbon dioxide. The notes present this comparison in a table. Exhaled air is also described as warm and moist.

options: Cold and dry
Warm and moist
Full of dust and germs
Rich in oxygen only
mcqs.q: Exhaled air is also described in the notes as being:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is warm and moist, because the notes add this description to exhaled air along with its higher carbon dioxide. Inhaled air is not described in this way. This is one of the clear differences between the air breathed in and the air breathed out.

options: A fall of carbon dioxide in the blood
A rise of carbon dioxide in the blood
A fall of oxygen need during exercise
Relaxation of the intercostal muscles
mcqs.q: What makes the breathing rate increase?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is a rise in carbon dioxide in the blood, which the notes say increases the breathing rate. A fall in carbon dioxide would not have this effect. The body breathes faster to remove the extra carbon dioxide.

options: Because the muscles need less energy during exercise
Because the chest capacity permanently decreases
Because the muscles need more energy, which needs more oxygen and produces more carbon dioxide to be removed
Because lactic acid stops being formed in the muscles
mcqs.q: Why does breathing become faster during or after exercise?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that during exercise the muscles need more energy, which needs more oxygen and produces more carbon dioxide to be removed. The notes give this as the reason breathing becomes faster during or after exercise. Faster breathing supplies the oxygen and clears the extra carbon dioxide.

options: The oxygen lost through exhaled air
The oxygen trapped by hairs and mucus in the nose
The oxygen used to warm and moisten inhaled air
The extra oxygen needed after hard exercise to remove the lactic acid formed in the muscles
mcqs.q: What is oxygen debt?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the extra oxygen needed afterwards to remove lactic acid. During hard exercise the muscles work without enough oxygen and lactic acid is formed. The notes call the extra oxygen required to clear that lactic acid the oxygen debt.

lessons.title: Breathing Disorders and Effects of Smoking
lessons.notes_html:
Emphysema

This disorder is linked to damage of the alveoli. In emphysema the walls of the alveoli break down and breathing becomes difficult.

Asthma

This disorder is linked to narrowing of the air passage. In asthma the air passage narrows and breathing becomes difficult.

To protect an asthma patient: avoid dust, smoke, cold air and other triggers, take medicine on time, live in a clean environment and follow the doctor's instructions.

Lung cancer

Lung cancer is the uncontrolled growth of cells in the lungs. It is mostly caused by smoking and makes breathing difficult.

Why is smoking harmful?

Cigarette smoke contains poisonous substances like nicotine, tar and carbon monoxide which damage the lungs and the air passage.

  • Disorders connected with smoking: bronchitis, emphysema, asthma and lung cancer.

Prevention of respiratory disorders

  • Avoid smoking.
  • Live in clean air and stay away from dust and smoke.
  • Exercise regularly and eat a balanced diet.
  • Get vaccinated.
  • Seek timely treatment if illness occurs.

options: Their walls break down and breathing becomes difficult
They become narrower air passages
They grow in an uncontrolled way
They are blocked by dust and cold air
mcqs.q: In emphysema, what happens to the alveoli?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that in emphysema the walls of the alveoli break down and breathing becomes difficult. The notes link this disorder directly to damage of the alveoli. Narrowing of the air passage describes asthma instead, not emphysema.

options: Damage and breakdown of the alveoli walls
Uncontrolled growth of cells in the lungs
Narrowing of the air passage
Poisoning by nicotine and tar only
mcqs.q: Asthma is a disorder linked to:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is narrowing of the air passage, because the notes state that in asthma the air passage narrows and breathing becomes difficult. Breakdown of alveoli walls is emphysema. Uncontrolled cell growth in the lungs is lung cancer.

options: Living in dusty and smoky air
Avoiding dust, smoke, cold air and other triggers, and taking medicine on time
Stopping all medicine when breathing feels normal
Exercising in cold smoky air every day
mcqs.q: Which step helps to protect an asthma patient?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is to avoid dust, smoke, cold air and other triggers, and to take medicine on time. The notes also advise a clean environment and following the doctor's instructions for an asthma patient. Dusty and smoky air would act as triggers and make the condition worse.

options: The narrowing of the air passage in the chest
The breakdown of the walls of the alveoli
An infection cured by vaccination alone
The uncontrolled growth of cells in the lungs
mcqs.q: What is lung cancer?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the uncontrolled growth of cells in the lungs, which is how the notes define lung cancer. It is mostly caused by smoking and makes breathing difficult. It is different from asthma and emphysema, which involve the air passage and alveoli walls.

options: Cold air
Smoking
Dust in the nose
Lack of exercise only
mcqs.q: What is lung cancer mostly caused by?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is smoking, because the notes state that lung cancer is mostly caused by smoking. Smoking also damages the lungs through the poisonous substances in cigarette smoke. This is why avoiding smoking is given as a key preventive step.

options: Oxygen, carbon dioxide and water vapour
Lactic acid, mucus and dust particles
Nicotine, tar and carbon monoxide
Germs, hairs and warm moist air
mcqs.q: Which poisonous substances are named in cigarette smoke?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is nicotine, tar and carbon monoxide, which the notes name as the poisonous substances in cigarette smoke. These substances damage the lungs and the air passage. Oxygen and carbon dioxide are normal gases of breathing, not the named poisons of smoke.

options: Bronchitis, emphysema, asthma and lung cancer
Only lung cancer alone
Oxygen debt and lactic acid formation
Gaseous exchange and ventilation disorders
mcqs.q: Which set of disorders is connected with smoking in the notes?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is bronchitis, emphysema, asthma and lung cancer, because the notes list all four as disorders connected with smoking. Smoking is therefore harmful in several ways at once. It damages both the lungs and the air passage.

options: Smoke regularly but exercise sometimes
Stay close to dust and smoke to build strength
Avoid smoking and live in clean air, away from dust and smoke
Delay treatment until the illness becomes severe
mcqs.q: Which is a correct way to prevent respiratory disorders?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is to avoid smoking and live in clean air, staying away from dust and smoke. The notes list these among the ways to prevent respiratory disorders. Delaying treatment is the opposite of the timely treatment the notes advise.

options: Eating an unbalanced diet and avoiding exercise
Exercising regularly and eating a balanced diet
Taking medicine only when a doctor is unavailable
Breathing through the mouth in dusty air
mcqs.q: Which habits are included in the prevention of respiratory disorders?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is exercising regularly and eating a balanced diet, both of which the notes include in prevention. A healthy lifestyle supports the respiratory system along with clean air and avoiding smoking. An unbalanced diet and no exercise go against this advice.

options: Ignore it and keep smoking
Wait for it to pass without any treatment
Get vaccinated only after the illness ends
Seek timely treatment, and also get vaccinated as a preventive step
mcqs.q: What should a person do if a respiratory illness occurs?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is to seek timely treatment if illness occurs, while vaccination is listed as a preventive step. The notes end their prevention list with getting vaccinated and seeking timely treatment. Ignoring an illness or delaying treatment is not advised anywhere in the lesson.

lessons.title: Introduction to Homeostasis and Homeostasis in Plants
lessons.notes_html:
What is homeostasis?

Keeping the internal condition of an organism steady is called homeostasis. In other words, the combined biological processes that keep the internal environment stable are homeostasis.

Why does the body need homeostasis?

Homeostasis is needed to keep the body's internal environment (temperature, water, salts and pH) steady so that the cells and organs can work properly.

Removal of extra water in plants

  • Transpiration: extra water leaves as vapour through the leaves.
  • Guttation: water leaves as drops from the leaf edges.
  • Excretion: plants also remove extra water by excretion.

Remember: the removal of extra water from the body in the form of vapour is called transpiration, not guttation.

Halophytes — plants of salty places

Plants growing in salty places like the seashore are halophytes, i.e. salt-tolerant plants.

They survive in salty water in these ways:

  • By storing salt in their cells.
  • By removing extra salt.
  • By keeping their water balance steady.

options: Keeping the internal condition of an organism steady
Removing extra water only through the leaves
Growing in salty places near the seashore
Changing the internal environment again and again
mcqs.q: What is homeostasis?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is keeping the internal condition of an organism steady. Homeostasis means the combined biological processes that keep the internal environment stable. It is about steadiness inside the body, not about changing that environment.

options: The colour of the skin
Temperature, water, salts and pH
The shape of the leaves
Only the amount of light around the body
mcqs.q: Which of these is part of the body's internal environment that homeostasis keeps steady?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is temperature, water, salts and pH. Homeostasis keeps these parts of the internal environment steady. This steadiness allows the cells and organs to work properly.

options: So that extra salt can be stored in the leaves
So that water can leave as drops from leaf edges
So that the cells and organs can work properly
So that the body temperature keeps rising
mcqs.q: Why does the body need homeostasis?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is so that the cells and organs can work properly. They need a steady internal environment of temperature, water, salts and pH. Without this steadiness, their normal working is disturbed.

options: Guttation
Excretion
Storage of salt
Transpiration
mcqs.q: In plants, extra water leaves as vapour through the leaves in which process?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is transpiration. In transpiration, extra water leaves the plant as vapour through the leaves. It must not be confused with guttation, where water leaves as drops.

options: Water leaving as drops from the leaf edges
Water leaving as vapour through the leaves
Salt being stored inside the cells
Water balance being kept steady in salty water
mcqs.q: What is guttation in plants?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is water leaving as drops from the leaf edges. This is guttation, and the form of the water is the key point. In transpiration, by contrast, the water leaves as vapour.

options: By sweating
By excretion
By widening blood vessels
By storing salt
mcqs.q: Besides transpiration and guttation, how else do plants remove extra water?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is by excretion. The notes state that plants also remove extra water by excretion, in addition to transpiration and guttation. Sweating and blood vessels belong to animals, not to this plant process.

options: Nephrons
Thermoregulators
Halophytes
Excretory plants only
mcqs.q: Plants growing in salty places like the seashore are called what?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is halophytes. Halophytes are salt-tolerant plants that grow in salty places such as the seashore. The name describes their ability to survive where there is much salt.

options: By producing more sweat
By narrowing their blood vessels
By changing their pH every day
By storing salt in their cells
mcqs.q: Which is one way halophytes survive in salty water?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is by storing salt in their cells. Storing salt in the cells is one of the ways halophytes survive in salty water. They also remove extra salt and keep their water balance steady.

options: Removing extra salt and keeping water balance steady
Producing sweat and cooling the body
Filtering blood and making urine
Leaving water as vapour and leaving water as drops only
mcqs.q: Which pair shows two ways halophytes survive in salty water?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is removing extra salt and keeping water balance steady. Both are listed as ways halophytes survive in salty water. Filtering blood and making urine are kidney functions, not halophyte adaptations.

options: Guttation
Transpiration
Excretion of salt
Homeostasis in animals
mcqs.q: The removal of extra water from the body in the form of vapour is called:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is transpiration, not guttation. The notes give this as a point to remember: water removed as vapour is transpiration. Guttation removes water as drops from the leaf edges.

lessons.title: Homeostasis in Animals and Humans
lessons.notes_html:
Skin — the largest organ

The skin is considered the largest organ of the human body. The skin is not just a covering; it also plays a big part in homeostasis.

What is thermoregulation?

Keeping the body temperature steady at a set level is called thermoregulation, and the process that keeps the temperature steady is also thermoregulation.

Layers of the skin and the dermis

The layer of the skin containing a network of blood vessels is called the dermis. The dermis contains the network of blood vessels, nerves and sweat glands.

Why is the skin an excretory organ?

The skin removes extra water, salts and waste substances like urea from the body through sweat, so it is considered an excretory organ.

What does the skin do in heat?

  • The blood vessels of the skin widen.
  • More sweat is produced.
  • The evaporation of sweat cools the body and the temperature stays steady.

What does the skin do in cold?

In cold the skin narrows the blood vessels and reduces sweating to conserve heat. In this way the skin works as a thermoregulatory organ: it cools the body in heat and conserves heat in cold.

options: The kidney
The bladder
The skin
The nephron
mcqs.q: Which is considered the largest organ of the human body?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the skin. The skin is considered the largest organ of the human body. It is not just a covering, because it also plays a big part in homeostasis.

options: Removing urea through sweat
Keeping the body temperature steady at a set level
Carrying urine to the bladder
Filtering the blood in the kidney
mcqs.q: What is thermoregulation?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is keeping the body temperature steady at a set level. That steady keeping of temperature is thermoregulation. Removing urea through sweat is excretion, which is a different skin function.

options: The dermis
The pelvis
The cortex
The medulla
mcqs.q: Which layer of the skin contains a network of blood vessels?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the dermis. The dermis is the layer of the skin containing a network of blood vessels. It also contains nerves and sweat glands.

options: Only the glomerulus and Bowman's capsule
Two kidneys and two ureters
Salt stored in plant cells
A network of blood vessels, nerves and sweat glands
mcqs.q: What does the dermis contain?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is a network of blood vessels, nerves and sweat glands. All three are found in the dermis of the skin. The glomerulus and Bowman's capsule belong to the nephron in the kidney.

options: Because it keeps the body temperature at a set level only
Because it removes extra water, salts and waste substances like urea through sweat
Because it is the largest organ of the body
Because it contains nerves
mcqs.q: Why is the skin considered an excretory organ?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is because it removes extra water, salts and waste substances like urea through sweat. Removing waste from the body is excretion. That is why the skin is considered an excretory organ.

options: They narrow
They disappear
They widen
They stop carrying blood
mcqs.q: What happens to the blood vessels of the skin in heat?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that they widen. In heat, the blood vessels of the skin widen and more sweat is produced. Narrowing of the blood vessels happens in cold, to conserve heat.

options: Its evaporation cools the body and the temperature stays steady
It stores heat inside the blood vessels
It removes urine from the bladder
It stops the dermis from working
mcqs.q: How does sweat help the body in heat?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that the evaporation of sweat cools the body and the temperature stays steady. In heat more sweat is produced for this cooling. This is one way the skin keeps the body temperature steady.

options: It widens the blood vessels and increases sweating
It produces urea in the kidney
It leaves water as drops from leaf edges
It narrows the blood vessels and reduces sweating
mcqs.q: What does the skin do in cold?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that it narrows the blood vessels and reduces sweating. Both actions conserve heat in cold conditions. Widening the vessels and producing more sweat happen in heat, not in cold.

options: Filters blood and makes urine
Cools the body in heat and conserves heat in cold
Stores urine before it leaves the body
Carries urine to the bladder
mcqs.q: The skin works as a thermoregulatory organ because it:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that it cools the body in heat and conserves heat in cold. These two opposite actions keep the body temperature steady. Filtering blood and making urine are the work of the kidney.

options: It is only a covering and has no part in homeostasis
It contains no sweat glands
It is not just a covering; it also plays a big part in homeostasis
It removes waste only through urine
mcqs.q: Which statement about the skin is correct?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that the skin is not just a covering and also plays a big part in homeostasis. It helps in temperature control and in excretion through sweat. Saying it has no part in homeostasis is the opposite of the notes.

lessons.title: Human Kidney and Structure of the Nephron
lessons.notes_html:
The kidney and its membrane

The kidney is enclosed in a membrane called the peritoneum.

Parts of the kidney and their work

PartWork / place
CortexOuter part
MedullaInner part
PelvisUrine-collecting part
NephronUnit that filters the blood and makes urine
UreterTube carrying urine to the bladder

The human urinary system

The human urinary system consists of two kidneys, two ureters, one bladder and one urethra.

Pathway: the kidneys make urine → the ureters carry it to the bladder → the bladder stores it → it leaves through the urethra.

Nephron — the unit of the kidney

The nephron is the unit of the kidney. It includes the glomerulus, Bowman's capsule, the proximal convoluted tubule, the loop of Henle, the distal convoluted tubule and the collecting duct. Its detailed functions are given in the next lesson.

options: Peritoneum
Dermis
Pelvis
Cortex
mcqs.q: The kidney is enclosed in a membrane called the:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the peritoneum. The kidney is enclosed in this membrane. The cortex, medulla and pelvis are parts inside the kidney, not the membrane around it.

options: The medulla
The cortex
The pelvis
The ureter
mcqs.q: Which part of the kidney is the outer part?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the cortex, which is the outer part of the kidney. The medulla is the inner part. The pelvis is the part that collects urine.

options: The cortex
The ureter
The medulla
The bladder
mcqs.q: Which part of the kidney is the inner part?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the medulla, the inner part of the kidney. The cortex is the outer part, so the two must not be mixed up. The bladder is a separate part of the urinary system that stores urine.

options: The cortex
The medulla
The peritoneum
The pelvis
mcqs.q: Which part of the kidney collects urine?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the pelvis, the urine-collecting part of the kidney. The cortex is the outer part and the medulla is the inner part. The peritoneum is the membrane enclosing the kidney.

options: The unit that filters the blood and makes urine
The tube carrying urine to the bladder
The membrane enclosing the kidney
The part that stores urine
mcqs.q: What is the nephron?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the unit that filters the blood and makes urine. The nephron is the unit of the kidney. The tube carrying urine to the bladder is the ureter, not the nephron.

options: To filter the blood
To carry urine to the bladder
To store urine for a long time
To enclose the kidney in a membrane
mcqs.q: What is the work of the ureter?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is to carry urine to the bladder. The kidneys make the urine and the ureters carry it onward. The bladder, not the ureter, is the part that stores urine.

options: One kidney, one ureter, two bladders and one urethra
Two kidneys, one ureter, one bladder and two urethras
Two kidneys, two ureters, one bladder and one urethra
Only the kidneys and the bladder
mcqs.q: The human urinary system consists of:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is two kidneys, two ureters, one bladder and one urethra. These four kinds of parts together make the human urinary system. The numbers of each part are an important part of the answer.

options: Bladder makes urine, then urethra carries it to the kidneys
Urethra makes urine, then ureter stores it
Kidneys store urine, then bladder makes it
Kidneys make urine, ureters carry it to the bladder, bladder stores it, it leaves through the urethra
mcqs.q: What is the correct pathway of urine in the urinary system?
mcqs.why: The correct answer follows the order: kidneys make urine, ureters carry it to the bladder, the bladder stores it, and it leaves through the urethra. Each part has its own step in this pathway. Reversing the order gives a wrong pathway.

options: The glomerulus
The peritoneum
The ureter
The bladder
mcqs.q: Which of these is a part of the nephron?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the glomerulus, which is included in the nephron. The nephron also includes Bowman's capsule, the tubules and the collecting duct. The ureter and bladder are parts of the urinary system outside the nephron.

options: Cortex, medulla and pelvis
Glomerulus, Bowman's capsule, proximal convoluted tubule, loop of Henle, distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct
Two kidneys, two ureters and one bladder
Blood vessels, nerves and sweat glands
mcqs.q: Which list gives parts included in the nephron?
mcqs.why: The correct answer lists the glomerulus, Bowman's capsule, the proximal convoluted tubule, the loop of Henle, the distal convoluted tubule and the collecting duct. These together make up the nephron. The other lists name kidney parts, urinary system parts or skin parts.

lessons.title: Functions of the Nephron and Formation of Urine
lessons.notes_html:
Structure of the nephron again

The nephron consists of the glomerulus (a ball of blood capillaries), Bowman's capsule, the proximal convoluted tubule, the loop of Henle and the distal convoluted tubule; the collecting duct is joined with it.

Steps of urine formation

Filtration of blood in the glomerulus → selective reabsorption in the tubule → tubular secretion → collection of urine in the collecting duct

Selective reabsorption

In the nephron, selective reabsorption takes place in the convoluted tubule. By reabsorption, useful substances like water, glucose and salts return to the blood.

Tubular secretion

By tubular secretion, extra and harmful substances move from the blood into the tubule so that they leave in the urine.

ProcessWhat happens?
ReabsorptionUseful substances: water, glucose, salts return to the blood
SecretionExtra and harmful substances from the blood into the tubule, then out with the urine

Role of the blood-vessel network

The glomerulus (a ball of blood capillaries) filters the blood; the network of blood vessels around the tubule takes reabsorbed substances back into the blood and supplies substances for secretion; thus the blood network plays the central role in making urine.

ADH hormone

The ADH hormone is secreted by the pituitary gland.

options: A tube that stores urine
A hormone from the pituitary gland
A ball of blood capillaries
A duct that collects urine only
mcqs.q: What is the glomerulus?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is a ball of blood capillaries. The glomerulus is the part of the nephron where the blood is filtered. It is a structure of capillaries, not a hormone or a storage tube.

options: Filtration in the glomerulus, selective reabsorption in the tubule, tubular secretion, collection in the collecting duct
Tubular secretion, collection, filtration, reabsorption
Collection in the collecting duct, filtration, secretion, reabsorption
Reabsorption, collection, filtration, secretion
mcqs.q: What is the correct order of the steps of urine formation?
mcqs.why: The correct answer starts with filtration of blood in the glomerulus, then selective reabsorption in the tubule, then tubular secretion, and finally collection of urine in the collecting duct. This is the order given for urine formation. Any other order mixes up the steps.

options: In the glomerulus
In the convoluted tubule
In the pituitary gland
In the bladder
mcqs.q: Where does selective reabsorption take place in the nephron?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is in the convoluted tubule. Selective reabsorption takes place there, returning useful substances to the blood. Filtration, not reabsorption, takes place in the glomerulus.

options: Only harmful substances
Extra substances from the tubule air
Water, glucose and salts
Urine collected in the duct
mcqs.q: By reabsorption, which useful substances return to the blood?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is water, glucose and salts. These are useful substances, so by reabsorption they return to the blood instead of leaving in the urine. Harmful and extra substances are handled by secretion, not reabsorption.

options: Useful substances return from the tubule to the blood
Blood is filtered in the glomerulus
Urine is stored in the bladder
Extra and harmful substances move from the blood into the tubule
mcqs.q: What happens in tubular secretion?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that extra and harmful substances move from the blood into the tubule. From there they leave in the urine. This is the opposite direction from reabsorption, where useful substances return to the blood.

options: Reabsorption: useful substances return to the blood; Secretion: extra and harmful substances go into the tubule
Reabsorption: harmful substances go into the tubule; Secretion: glucose returns to the blood
Reabsorption: urine is collected; Secretion: blood is filtered
Reabsorption and secretion both store urine
mcqs.q: Which pairing is correct?
mcqs.why: The correct answer pairs reabsorption with useful substances returning to the blood, and secretion with extra and harmful substances moving into the tubule. The two processes work in opposite directions. Swapping them makes the pairing wrong.

options: It secretes the ADH hormone
It takes reabsorbed substances back into the blood and supplies substances for secretion
It stores urine before excretion
It carries urine to the bladder
mcqs.q: What does the network of blood vessels around the tubule do?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that it takes reabsorbed substances back into the blood and supplies substances for secretion. Because of this double role, the blood vessel network plays the central role in making urine. Carrying urine to the bladder is the work of the ureter.

options: The collecting duct
The distal convoluted tubule only
The glomerulus
The pituitary gland
mcqs.q: Which part filters the blood at the start of urine formation?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the glomerulus, a ball of blood capillaries that filters the blood. Filtration in the glomerulus is the first step of urine formation. The collecting duct only collects the urine at the end.

options: The sweat gland
The kidney's cortex
The skin's dermis
The pituitary gland
mcqs.q: The ADH hormone is secreted by which gland?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the pituitary gland, which secretes the ADH hormone. Sweat glands are found in the dermis of the skin and do not secrete ADH. The cortex is a part of the kidney, not a gland secreting this hormone.

options: In the collecting duct
In the glomerulus
In the pituitary gland
In Bowman's capsule as stored urine
mcqs.q: Where is urine collected after tubular secretion?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the collecting duct, where urine is collected as the last step of urine formation. The steps before it are filtration, selective reabsorption and tubular secretion. The glomerulus belongs to the first step, filtration.

lessons.title: Disorders of the Excretory System and Kidney Stones
lessons.notes_html:
Kidney diseases

  • Kidney stones
  • Nephritis — inflammation of the kidney
  • Urinary tract infection
  • Kidney failure

Methods of treatment

  • Medicines
  • Breaking up stones — lithotripsy — or surgery
  • Dialysis
  • Kidney transplant

Why is dialysis needed?

When the kidneys fail and cannot remove waste substances and extra water from the blood, dialysis is needed to clean the blood with a machine.

Remember: dialysis does the kidney's work by a machine, in a transplant the kidney is replaced, and lithotripsy is for breaking stones — the three treatments are for different conditions.

options: Breaking up of kidney stones
Inflammation of the kidney
Cleaning of blood by a machine
Replacement of the kidney
mcqs.q: Nephritis is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is inflammation of the kidney. Nephritis is listed among the kidney diseases with this meaning. Breaking up stones is lithotripsy, and cleaning blood by a machine is dialysis.

options: Kidney stones
Thermoregulation
Guttation
Selective reabsorption
mcqs.q: Which of these is listed as a disorder of the excretory system?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is kidney stones, which are listed among the kidney diseases. Nephritis, urinary tract infection and kidney failure are the other disorders listed. The other options here are normal processes, not disorders.

options: Transpiration, guttation and excretion
Filtration, reabsorption and secretion
Kidney stones, nephritis, urinary tract infection and kidney failure
Cortex, medulla, pelvis and nephron
mcqs.q: Which list contains only disorders named in this lesson?
mcqs.why: The correct answer lists kidney stones, nephritis, urinary tract infection and kidney failure. These are the kidney diseases named in the lesson. The other lists name plant processes, urine-formation steps or kidney parts.

options: Replacing a failed kidney
Cleaning the blood when kidneys fail
Treating inflammation by storing urine
Breaking up kidney stones
mcqs.q: Lithotripsy is a treatment used for:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is breaking up kidney stones. Lithotripsy, or surgery, is the method named for breaking up stones. Dialysis cleans the blood and a transplant replaces the kidney, so those are different treatments.

options: When the kidneys fail and cannot remove waste substances and extra water from the blood
When water leaves as drops from leaf edges
When the skin produces more sweat in heat
When a stone is first formed in the bladder only
mcqs.q: When is dialysis needed?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is when the kidneys fail and cannot remove waste substances and extra water from the blood. Dialysis is then needed to clean the blood with a machine. It does the kidney's cleaning work when the kidneys themselves cannot.

options: It replaces the kidney with a new one
It cleans the blood with a machine, doing the kidney's work
It breaks up stones inside the kidney
It carries urine from the kidney to the bladder
mcqs.q: What does dialysis do?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that dialysis cleans the blood with a machine, doing the kidney's work. In a transplant the kidney is replaced, which is a different treatment. Lithotripsy, not dialysis, breaks up stones.

options: The blood is cleaned by a machine
Stones are broken up
The kidney is replaced
Urine is collected in a duct
mcqs.q: In a kidney transplant, what happens?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that the kidney is replaced. That is what a transplant means in this lesson. Dialysis cleans the blood by machine and lithotripsy breaks stones, so they must not be confused with a transplant.

options: Dialysis for breaking stones
Lithotripsy for cleaning blood by machine
Transplant for making urine in the nephron
Lithotripsy for breaking stones, dialysis for failed kidneys, transplant for replacing the kidney
mcqs.q: Which treatment is matched correctly with its condition?
mcqs.why: The correct answer matches lithotripsy with breaking stones, dialysis with failed kidneys and transplant with replacing the kidney. The lesson stresses that these three treatments are for different conditions. Mixing their uses makes a pairing wrong.

options: Medicines
Transpiration
Thermoregulation
Homeostasis
mcqs.q: Which of these is listed as a method of treatment for excretory system disorders?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is medicines, which are listed among the methods of treatment. The other methods named are breaking up stones by lithotripsy or surgery, dialysis and kidney transplant. Transpiration and homeostasis are processes, not treatments.

options: Dialysis
Surgery
Transplant
Medicines through sweat
mcqs.q: Besides lithotripsy, which other method is named for dealing with kidney stones?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is surgery, named together with lithotripsy for breaking up stones. Dialysis and transplant are treatments for kidney failure and kidney replacement. They are not the methods named for stones.

lessons.title: Types of Coordination and the Neuron
lessons.notes_html:
What is coordination?

Coordination means the parts of the body working together in an orderly way. A change in the environment is called a stimulus, and the movement made in answer to that change is called a response.

  • Stimulus: a change in the environment.
  • Receptor: the part that perceives the stimulus.
  • Response: the movement made in answer to the stimulus.
  • Effector: the part that responds, such as a muscle.

Two types of coordination

TypeMethodSpeed and duration
NervousThrough electrochemical signalsFast, for a short time
ChemicalThrough hormones, by the bloodSlow, long-lasting

A hormone is a chemical released from one cell that signals another cell at a distance, or is sent through the blood.

Why is nervous coordination faster?

Nervous coordination travels directly and fast through electrochemical signals, while in chemical coordination hormones travel slowly through the blood.

Coordination in plants

Coordination in plants takes place chemically, through hormones. Plants have no nervous system.

Which system is better?

Both systems are necessary in their place; the nervous system acts fast and briefly, while the chemical (endocrine) system acts slowly but for a long time, so together they work best.

Feedback system

A feedback system is one in which the result of an action is reported back to the system so that the action can be increased or decreased and balance is maintained.

Note: three types of neurons are named in this chapter's questions — the sensory neuron, the intermediate neuron and the motor neuron — and they are explained in detail in the reflex action lesson. The signal passes from the receptor through the sensory neuron to the spinal cord and then through the motor neuron to the effector.

options: The movement of a single muscle alone
The parts of the body working together in an orderly way
The release of hormones into the blood
A change in the environment
mcqs.q: What is coordination?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that the parts of the body work together in an orderly way. The notes define coordination in exactly this way. A single muscle movement or a change in the environment alone is not coordination.

options: The part that responds, such as a muscle
The movement made in answer to a change
A change in the environment
The part that perceives a change
mcqs.q: What is a stimulus?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is a change in the environment. The notes define a stimulus as a change in the environment. The movement made in answer to that change is called the response, not the stimulus.

options: The part that perceives the stimulus
The movement made in answer to the stimulus
A chemical sent through the blood
The muscle that responds to a signal
mcqs.q: What is a receptor?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the part that perceives the stimulus. The notes state this definition of a receptor directly. The part that responds is the effector, while the movement itself is the response.

options: The spinal cord
A sensory neuron
The eye
A muscle
mcqs.q: Which of the following is an example of an effector?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is a muscle. The notes describe the effector as the part that responds, such as a muscle. The receptor perceives the stimulus, but the effector carries out the response.

options: Through hormones carried slowly by the blood
Through electrochemical signals, fast and for a short time
Through the blood only, with long-lasting effects
Without any signals between body parts
mcqs.q: How does nervous coordination work?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is through electrochemical signals, fast and for a short time. The notes contrast this with chemical coordination, which is slow and long-lasting. Nervous coordination is therefore the rapid, short-lived type.

options: Through hormones, by the blood, slow and long-lasting
Through electrochemical signals, fast and brief
Through neurons directly to muscles
Only through the spinal cord
mcqs.q: How does chemical coordination work?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is through hormones by the blood, slow and long-lasting. The notes give this as the method, speed and duration of chemical coordination. Electrochemical signals belong to nervous coordination instead.

options: An electrochemical signal in a neuron
The part that perceives a stimulus
A chemical released from one cell that signals another cell at a distance, or is sent through the blood
The movement made in answer to a stimulus
mcqs.q: What is a hormone?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is a chemical released from one cell that signals another cell at a distance, or is sent through the blood. This is the definition given in the notes. It is different from a stimulus, a receptor or a response.

options: Because hormones travel faster than nerve signals
Because both systems use the blood at the same speed
Because plants have no nervous system
Because it travels directly and fast through electrochemical signals, while hormones travel slowly through the blood
mcqs.q: Why is nervous coordination faster than chemical coordination?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that nervous coordination travels directly and fast through electrochemical signals, while hormones travel slowly through the blood. The notes explain the speed difference in exactly this way. That is why nervous responses are quicker.

options: Chemically, through hormones, because plants have no nervous system
Through a nervous system like animals
Through electrochemical signals in neurons
Plants show no coordination at all
mcqs.q: How does coordination take place in plants?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is chemically, through hormones, because plants have no nervous system. The notes state this clearly for plants. Plants therefore depend only on chemical coordination.

options: A system in which hormones are stored in glands
A system found only in plants
A system in which the result of an action is reported back so the action can be increased or decreased and balance is maintained
A system in which the brain thinks before every movement
mcqs.q: What is a feedback system?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is a system in which the result of an action is reported back so the action can be increased or decreased and balance is maintained. The notes define a feedback system in this way. Its purpose is to maintain balance in the body.

lessons.title: Human Nervous System and Its Parts
lessons.notes_html:
Main parts of the human brain

PartWork
CerebrumLargest part, thinking and memory
CerebellumBalance and precision of movement
Brain stem (medulla, pons, midbrain)Basic actions like breathing and heartbeat

The brain is covered by three meninges membranes and has ventricles inside.

Frontal lobe

The frontal lobe of the cerebrum is connected with reasoning, thinking and decision-making.

Parts of the nervous system

  • Central Nervous System (CNS)
  • Peripheral Nervous System (PNS)
  • Somatic system
  • Autonomic system — controls survival actions like heartbeat and breathing.

Why do people differ in intelligence?

Intelligence depends not only on the parts of the brain but on the number of neurons, the connections between them, the growth of the brain, education and environment; differences in these cause differences in intelligence.

options: Cerebellum — balance and precision of movement
Cerebrum — thinking and memory
Brain stem — breathing and heartbeat
Frontal lobe — decision-making only
mcqs.q: Which is the largest part of the human brain and what is its work?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the cerebrum, which is the largest part and is concerned with thinking and memory. The notes list the cerebellum for balance and the brain stem for basic actions. The cerebrum is therefore distinct from both.

options: Thinking and memory
Reasoning and decision-making
Balance and precision of movement
Breathing and heartbeat
mcqs.q: What is the work of the cerebellum?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is balance and precision of movement. The notes assign this work to the cerebellum. Thinking and memory belong to the cerebrum, while breathing and heartbeat belong to the brain stem.

options: Basic actions like breathing and heartbeat
Thinking and memory only
Balance of movement only
Reasoning and decision-making
mcqs.q: What does the brain stem control?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is basic actions like breathing and heartbeat. The notes state that the brain stem, made of medulla, pons and midbrain, controls such basic actions. Thinking and memory are the work of the cerebrum instead.

options: Cerebrum, cerebellum and frontal lobe
Sclera, cornea and retina
Sensory, intermediate and motor neurons
Medulla, pons and midbrain
mcqs.q: Which parts make up the brain stem?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is medulla, pons and midbrain. The notes name these three as the parts of the brain stem. The cerebrum and cerebellum are separate parts of the brain, not parts of the brain stem.

options: By a single membrane, with no spaces inside
By three meninges membranes, with ventricles inside
By the sclera, with a lens inside
By hormones carried in the blood
mcqs.q: By what is the brain covered, and what does it have inside?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that the brain is covered by three meninges membranes and has ventricles inside. The notes state both facts together. The sclera and lens belong to the eye, not to the brain.

options: Reasoning, thinking and decision-making
Balance and precision only
Heartbeat and breathing only
Perceiving light stimuli only
mcqs.q: With what is the frontal lobe of the cerebrum connected?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is reasoning, thinking and decision-making. The notes connect the frontal lobe of the cerebrum with these functions. Balance belongs to the cerebellum and basic actions belong to the brain stem.

options: Somatic system and autonomic system only
Sensory system and motor system
Central Nervous System (CNS) and Peripheral Nervous System (PNS)
Nervous system and endocrine system
mcqs.q: Which are the two main divisions of the nervous system named in the notes?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the Central Nervous System (CNS) and the Peripheral Nervous System (PNS). The notes list these as the parts of the nervous system. The somatic and autonomic systems are also named, but CNS and PNS are the main divisions.

options: Thinking and memory
Voluntary writing movements only
Reasoning and decision-making
Survival actions like heartbeat and breathing
mcqs.q: What does the autonomic system control?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is survival actions like heartbeat and breathing. The notes describe the autonomic system in exactly this way. Thinking, memory and reasoning are functions of the cerebrum and its frontal lobe.

options: Only on the size of the cerebellum
On the number of neurons, connections between them, growth of the brain, education and environment
Only on hormones in the blood
Only on the three meninges membranes
mcqs.q: According to the notes, on what does intelligence depend?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the number of neurons, the connections between them, the growth of the brain, education and environment. The notes state that intelligence depends on all these factors, not on brain parts alone. Differences in these factors cause differences in intelligence.

options: Because only some people have a cerebrum
Because only some people have ventricles in the brain
Because of differences in neurons, their connections, brain growth, education and environment
Because of differences in the colour of the iris
mcqs.q: Why do people differ in intelligence, according to the notes?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is differences in neurons, their connections, brain growth, education and environment. The notes explain that differences in these cause differences in intelligence. All people have a cerebrum, so that cannot explain the difference.

lessons.title: Reflex Action and Reflex Arc
lessons.notes_html:
What is a reflex action?

A reflex action is the quick response that takes place without the brain thinking. When a stimulus comes, the body moves at once.

Reflex arc — the pathway of the signal

Stimulus → receptor → sensory neuron → spinal cord → motor neuron → effector (muscle) → immediate movement

  • The stimulus is felt by the receptor.
  • The signal travels through a sensory neuron to the spinal cord.
  • From there it travels through a motor neuron to the effector (muscle).
  • The muscle moves at once, without the brain having to think.

How many neurons?

A reflex action usually involves three neurons: sensory neuron, intermediate neuron and motor neuron. The answer given in the book is at most three neurons.

options: A slow action planned by the brain
The quick response that takes place without the brain thinking
The release of a hormone into the blood
A response controlled only by the cerebellum
mcqs.q: What is a reflex action?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the quick response that takes place without the brain thinking. The notes define a reflex action in exactly this way. When a stimulus comes, the body moves at once without waiting for thought.

options: Stimulus, effector, motor neuron, spinal cord, sensory neuron, receptor
Stimulus, brain, receptor, muscle, spinal cord
Stimulus, receptor, sensory neuron, spinal cord, motor neuron, effector, immediate movement
Receptor, hormone, blood, effector, movement
mcqs.q: What is the correct pathway of the signal in a reflex arc?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is stimulus to receptor to sensory neuron to spinal cord to motor neuron to effector, followed by immediate movement. The notes give the reflex arc in this exact order. Hormones and the blood play no part in this pathway.

options: The receptor
The motor neuron
The effector muscle
The hormone
mcqs.q: In a reflex action, what feels the stimulus?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the receptor. The notes state that the stimulus is felt by the receptor at the start of the reflex arc. The signal then travels onward through the sensory neuron to the spinal cord.

options: Through the motor neuron
Through the intermediate neuron only
Through the optic nerve
Through a sensory neuron
mcqs.q: Through which neuron does the signal travel to the spinal cord in a reflex action?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is a sensory neuron. The notes state that the signal travels through a sensory neuron to the spinal cord. From the spinal cord it then travels through a motor neuron to the effector.

options: Through a sensory neuron
Through a motor neuron
Through a photoreceptor cell
Through no neuron, only through blood
mcqs.q: Through which neuron does the signal travel from the spinal cord to the effector?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is a motor neuron. The notes state that from the spinal cord the signal travels through a motor neuron to the effector, which is the muscle. The sensory neuron carries the signal in the opposite direction, towards the spinal cord.

options: The muscle moves at once, without the brain having to think
The muscle waits for a hormone to arrive
The muscle sends the stimulus to the receptor
The muscle stores the signal in the spinal cord
mcqs.q: What happens at the effector in a reflex action?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that the muscle moves at once, without the brain having to think. The notes describe the effector response in exactly this way. This immediate movement is what makes the action a reflex.

options: One neuron only
Two neurons only
Three neurons: sensory, intermediate and motor
Five neurons
mcqs.q: How many neurons does a reflex action usually involve?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is three neurons: the sensory neuron, the intermediate neuron and the motor neuron. The notes state that a reflex action usually involves these three. The book answer is at most three neurons.

options: Rod, cone and sensory neurons
Sensory, intermediate and motor neurons
Cerebrum, cerebellum and brain stem neurons
Frontal, autonomic and somatic neurons
mcqs.q: Which set names the three neurons involved in a reflex action?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is sensory, intermediate and motor neurons. The notes name exactly these three for a reflex action. Rods and cones are photoreceptor cells in the retina, not neurons of the reflex arc.

lessons.title: Endocrine System and Important Glands
lessons.notes_html:
What is the endocrine system?

The endocrine system is the system of glands that release hormones into the blood. Hormones reach the target organs through the blood and act there.

How does blood glucose stay steady?

  • When blood glucose rises, the pancreas releases insulin, which lowers it.
  • When glucose falls, it releases glucagon, which raises it.
  • In this way the level stays steady — this is an example of feedback.

Islets of Langerhans

The islets of Langerhans in the pancreas make the hormones insulin and glucagon, which control the blood glucose level.

Thyroid and goitre

Due to iodine deficiency the thyroid gland swells, which is called goitre.

Emergency hormones

The emergency hormones are adrenaline and noradrenaline, called the hormones of the adrenal glands. They prepare the body in times of danger.

FSH and LH

Gonads (sex glands) are the target organs of both FSH and LH — both hormones act on the gonads.

Diabetes (sugar)

Diabetes (sugar) is the disease in which blood glucose rises due to lack of insulin or its failure to act. Prevention: a balanced diet, exercise, keeping weight under control and regular check-ups.

lessons.title: Concept of Support and Movement and Types of Bones
lessons.notes_html:
What is movement?

When an organism feels restlessness due to a stimulus, i.e. an outside effect, that restlessness is removed by movement. Organisms move to remove the restlessness.

What is a skeleton?

The framework that gives a structure a firm shape is called the skeleton. The skeleton is the framework of bones and it gives the body a firm shape. The human skeleton is made of 206 bones.

Important functions of the skeleton

  • Giving the body shape and support
  • Protecting the internal organs, such as the brain, heart and lungs
  • Helping movement together with the muscles
  • Making blood cells
  • Storing minerals like calcium

The strength of the skeleton is due to the hard structure of bones, so the skeleton is called a strong system.

Difference between bone and cartilage

BoneCartilage

Cells and places of cartilage

The cell of cartilage is called a chondrocyte. These cells are quite different from bone cells. Cartilage is found in the places where flexibility is needed.

  • Cartilage is present on the surfaces of joints

lessons.title: The Human Skeleton: Axial and Appendicular Bones
lessons.notes_html:
The human skeleton

The human skeleton is a strong framework of 206 bones. It gives the body shape and support and produces movement together with the muscles. Its two big parts must be understood: the axial skeleton and the appendicular skeleton.

Sacrum and pelvic girdle

The sacral vertebrae join with the pelvic girdle. This joint helps to connect the legs with the central part of the body.

Bones of the leg and foot

Each leg and foot has these bones:

  • Femur: the thigh bone, known as the largest bone of the leg
  • Tibia and fibula: the two shin bones
  • Patella: the knee cap
  • Tarsals: 7 ankle bones
  • Metatarsals: 5 bones
  • Phalanges: 14 toe bones

lessons.title: Joints and Muscle Movement
lessons.notes_html:
What is a joint and its types

The place where two bones meet is called a joint. There are three big types in the human body:

  • Fixed or immovable joints: do not move at all, e.g. between the bones of the skull and between the teeth and the jaws
  • Cartilaginous or slightly movable joints: slight movement takes place, e.g. between the ribs and the vertebrae
  • Synovial or freely movable joints: free movement takes place

Types of synovial joints

JointMovementExample
Hinge jointMovement in one directionKnee and elbow
Ball-and-socket jointMovement in all directionsShoulder and hip
Pivot jointRotating movementNeck
Gliding jointSliding movementWrist and ankle

In a ball-and-socket joint the round head (ball) of one bone fits into the cup-like hollow (socket) of another bone, so the shoulder and hip joints can move in every direction.

Ligament and tendon

LigamentTendon
Joins bone to boneJoins muscle to bone
Is a strong band at a jointCarries the muscle's pull to the bone

Muscle movement: flexion and extension

Flexion → a muscle contracts and the joint bends, e.g. bending the arm. Extension → the opposite muscle contracts and the joint straightens, e.g. straightening the arm. The movement that straightens a joint is called extension.

Antagonist muscles

The pair of muscles working in opposite directions on one bone is called the antagonist pair. Biceps and triceps are its best example:

  • Biceps: the muscle with two heads, bends the arm
  • Triceps: the muscle with three heads, straightens the arm
  • The big muscle of the thigh is the quadriceps (tetraceps)

When one muscle contracts the other relaxes, so movement is smooth.

options: The place where two bones meet

A strong band at a joint
The cell of cartilage
mcqs.q: What is a joint?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the place where two bones meet. The notes define a joint in exactly this way. A muscle joining a bone describes the work of a tendon, and a strong band at a joint describes a ligament, so those choices are different structures.

lessons.title: Disorders of the Skeletal System
lessons.notes_html:
Bone disorder: rickets

Rickets is a disease of children in which the bones become soft and weak. A healthy bone is hard and strong, but in rickets the bone loses its hardness.

Cause of rickets

  • Deficiency of vitamin D is the biggest cause
  • Deficiency of calcium is also a cause
  • Deficiency of phosphorus is also a cause

Softening of children's bones due to vitamin D deficiency is called rickets. Calcium and phosphorus are the minerals needed for the strength of bones, and the skeleton also stores calcium.

Difference from other names

lessons.title: Sexual Reproduction in Plants
lessons.notes_html:
Sexual reproduction in plants and the flower

Reproduction is the process necessary for the survival of organisms and the continuation of life. In sexual reproduction a new organism is formed by the fusion of male and female gametes, and new combinations are produced in it, which are necessary for evolution.

Parts of an angiosperm flower

  • Sepals: together form the calyx
  • Petals: together form the corolla
  • Stamen: the male part, with anther and filament
  • Carpel: the female part, with stigma, style and ovary

Pollination

Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma. The series of the process is: anther → pollen grain → stigma → fertilisation → seed and fruit. Characteristics of insect-pollinated plants:

  • Flowers are colourful
  • Flowers are fragrant
  • Flowers are nectar-bearing, i.e. they have nectar
  • They have sticky pollen

Male and female gametophytes

The male gametophyte is the pollen grain. It has an outer coat (exine), an inner coat (intine), a tube cell and a generative cell; the generative cell forms two male gametes. The female gametophyte is the embryo sac.

Structure of the ovule

  • Outer coats: integuments
  • Micropyle: a small opening
  • Nucellus: the inner part
  • Embryo sac: the female gametophyte

Double fertilisation and endosperm

In angiosperms the endosperm is formed from the 3N zygote, i.e. triple fusion, which feeds the seed. The seed coat and the embryo are separate parts from it; the cotyledon is also separate from the endosperm.

Life cycle and seed germination

The life cycle of angiosperms: seed → germination → plant → flower → pollination → fertilisation → seed and fruit → seed again. Seed germination is the process in which a new plant emerges from the seed; it needs water, suitable temperature and oxygen.

EpigealHypogeal
Seed leaves come above the groundSeed leaves stay in the ground

options: By the division of a single cell into two parts

mcqs.why: The correct answer is the fusion of male and female gametes. The notes state that in sexual reproduction a new organism is formed by this fusion. This fusion also produces new combinations in the organism, which are necessary for evolution.

mcqs.why: The correct answer is the calyx. The notes state clearly that the sepals together form the calyx. The petals, not the sepals, together form the corolla, so the other options do not match the flower's structure.

lessons.title: Asexual Reproduction in Plants
lessons.notes_html:
Asexual and vegetative reproduction

In asexual reproduction a new organism is formed from a single parent without gametes. Vegetative propagation is its special form in which a new plant is formed from a part of the plant such as the stem, root or leaf.

Sexual reproductionAsexual reproductionVegetative propagation
A new organism is formed by the fusion of male and female gametesA new organism is formed from one parent without gametesA new plant is formed from a part of the plant (stem, root, leaf)

Methods of asexual reproduction in plants

  • Runner: a stem spreading on the ground
  • Rhizome: an underground stem like ginger
  • Tuber: a thick stem like potato
  • Bulb: a round structure like onion
  • Sucker: a stem arising from the root region of the mother plant
  • Budding, spores and tissue culture are also methods

Mint reproduces vegetatively by a stem creeping on the ground with little nourishment; this is an example of the runner method. Single-celled organisms also reproduce asexually without fusion by means of spores.

Apomixis

The method of seed production without male-female fusion is apomixis. In it a seed is formed but the fusion of fertilisation does not take place. Parthenocarpy and parthenogenesis are different terms from it.

How does a new plant obtain food?

At first a new plant gets food stored in the parent plant or the seed, then it takes in water and minerals through the roots and makes its own food by photosynthesis in the leaves.

By fertilisation inside an ovule
mcqs.q: In asexual reproduction, how is a new organism formed?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that a new organism is formed from a single parent without gametes. The notes give this as the definition of asexual reproduction. Fusion of male and female gametes describes sexual reproduction, which is a different process.

mcqs.why: The correct answer is the method of seed production without male-female fusion. The notes state that in apomixis a seed is formed but the fusion of fertilisation does not take place. Parthenocarpy and parthenogenesis are noted as different terms from apomixis.

lessons.title: Reproduction in Animals
lessons.notes_html:
Introduction to reproduction in animals

Reproduction in animals is both sexual and asexual. In sexual reproduction male and female gametes fuse, while in asexual reproduction new organisms are formed from a single organism without fusion.

Methods of asexual reproduction in animals

BuddingHydraA small outgrowth on the body becomes a new organism
FragmentationPlanariaA new organism is formed from a piece of the body

Remember that plant methods like runner, rhizome and bulb do not apply to animals. Remember four names for animals: binary fission, budding, fragmentation and parthenogenesis, together with their examples.

Note: the source has few facts for this lesson — all four methods are given in one detailed answer, so the whole lesson is built around these four methods and their examples.
