lessons.title: Sexual Reproduction in Humans: Male and Female Reproductive Systems
lessons.notes_html:
Sexual reproduction in humans

Sexual reproduction in humans takes place by the fusion of male and female gametes. The male gamete is the sperm and the female gamete is the ovum. The organs and glands of both systems must be understood separately.

Male reproductive system

  • Testes: the male gonads, present in the scrotal sac
  • Epididymis: a part joined with the testis
  • Vas deferens: the tube carrying sperms
  • Seminal vesicle: a gland
  • Prostate gland: a gland
  • Cowper's glands: glands
  • Penis: the external organ

The male gonad, i.e. the testis, is located in the scrotal sac.

Spermatogenesis

The process of sperm formation is called spermatogenesis. The series: seminiferous tubules of the testes → primary spermatocyte → meiosis → four haploid spermatids → mature sperms, i.e. from one primary spermatocyte four sperms are formed.

Female system and ovulation

The female gametes, i.e. ova, are released from the ovary. The release of the ovum is called ovulation. Ova are not released from the fallopian tube or the uterus; they come out only from the ovary.

What is STD?

STD (sexually transmitted diseases) are diseases spread from one person to another through sexual contact, such as gonorrhoea, syphilis and AIDS.

mcqs.why: The correct answer is that the male gamete is the sperm and the female gamete is the ovum. The notes state this directly for sexual reproduction in humans. This reproduction takes place by the fusion of these male and female gametes.

The external organ
mcqs.q: The epididymis in the male reproductive system is described as what?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is a part joined with the testis. The notes list the epididymis in this way among the parts of the male reproductive system. The tube carrying sperms is the vas deferens, and the penis is named as the external organ.

lessons.title: Population Planning
lessons.notes_html:
Population and reproduction

Reproduction is necessary for the survival of organisms and the continuation of life, so every generation goes forward. But in humans, when the population grows too much, pressure falls on resources, so population control becomes necessary.

Effects of population growth

  • Pressure on food increases
  • Pressure on water increases
  • Shortage of housing increases
  • Pressure on education increases
  • Pressure on health facilities increases
  • Pressure on jobs increases

Benefits of control

With population control, resources become enough for everyone and the society becomes successful. When people are fewer and resources are enough, every family easily gets food, water, housing, education, health and jobs.

Understand the series: population growth → pressure on resources → shortage and problems. Its opposite: population control → resources enough → successful society.

Note: for this lesson the direct facts in the source are in one detailed answer, together with the basic points of the importance of reproduction; so the centre of the lesson is this relation of pressure and control.

options: Because reproduction stops completely in humans
Because when population grows too much, pressure falls on resources
Because resources increase faster than population always
Because every family refuses food and housing
mcqs.q: Why does population control become necessary in humans, according to the notes?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that when the population grows too much, pressure falls on resources. The notes say reproduction is necessary for survival, but excessive population growth makes control necessary. The pressure on resources is the reason given, not a stop in reproduction.

options: Population growth leads to pressure on resources, then shortage and problems
Population growth leads to resources being enough, then a successful society
Population control leads to pressure on resources, then shortage
Population growth removes all pressure from food and water
mcqs.q: Which series correctly shows the result of population growth, according to the notes?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is population growth leading to pressure on resources, then shortage and problems. The notes ask us to understand the series in exactly this order. The opposite series, with resources enough and a successful society, belongs to population control.

options: Only on transport and entertainment
Only on sports and tourism
On food and on water
Only on clothing and vehicles
mcqs.q: Population growth increases pressure on which pair of basic needs, as listed in the notes?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is food and water. The notes list increased pressure on food and increased pressure on water among the effects of population growth. The same list also includes housing, education, health facilities and jobs.

options: Housing becomes free for everyone
Every family builds a larger house easily
Housing pressure disappears completely
Shortage of housing increases
mcqs.q: Which housing effect of population growth is stated in the notes?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that shortage of housing increases. The notes list this directly among the effects of population growth, alongside pressure on food, water, education, health facilities and jobs. Growth is therefore linked to shortage, not to easier housing.

options: Education
Only private transport
Only foreign travel
Only entertainment centres
mcqs.q: According to the notes, population growth also increases pressure on which service?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is education. The notes state that pressure on education increases as a result of population growth. Health facilities and jobs are also in the same list of things that come under increased pressure.

options: Pressure on rainfall and on weather
Pressure on forests and on oceans only
Pressure on health facilities and pressure on jobs
Pressure on sports grounds and on cinemas
mcqs.q: Which pair of pressures is included in the effects of population growth in the notes?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is pressure on health facilities and pressure on jobs. Both items appear in the notes' list of the effects of population growth. That list covers food, water, housing, education, health facilities and jobs.

options: Resources become enough for everyone and the society becomes successful
Shortage and problems increase further
Pressure on food and water rises sharply
Every family loses access to education and health
mcqs.q: With population control, what happens, according to the notes?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that resources become enough for everyone and the society becomes successful. The notes present this as the benefit of population control. It is the opposite of the shortage and problems caused by unchecked population growth.

options: Only food, but nothing else
Only jobs, but no housing
Only water, but no education
Food, water, housing, education, health and jobs
mcqs.q: When people are fewer and resources are enough, what does every family easily get, according to the notes?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is food, water, housing, education, health and jobs. The notes state that when people are fewer and resources are enough, every family easily gets all of these. These are the same needs that come under pressure when population grows too much.

options: Only for increasing pressure on resources
For the survival of organisms and the continuation of life
Only for causing shortage of housing
Only for spreading diseases in a population
mcqs.q: Reproduction itself is described in the notes as necessary for what?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is for the survival of organisms and the continuation of life. The notes begin with this importance of reproduction, so that every generation goes forward. Population planning is about controlling excessive growth, not about denying this basic role of reproduction.

options: Population control leads to resources enough, then a successful society
Population growth leads to pressure on resources, then shortage
More population leads to more shortage and more problems
Population control leads to pressure on jobs and health
mcqs.q: Which series correctly shows the opposite, beneficial direction described in the notes?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is population control leading to resources being enough and then a successful society. The notes set this series as the opposite of growth leading to pressure and shortage. Control is therefore linked to sufficiency, not to increased pressure.

lessons.title: Introduction to Inheritance: Chromosomes and Genes
lessons.notes_html:
Genetics and inheritance

The branch of biology that studies heredity and variation is called genetics. The way parents transfer their genes to offspring is called inheritance.

Chromosome and chromatin

In each cell, each chromosome is a thread-like structure. The centre part of a chromosome, where the two chromatids are joined, is called the centromere. The chemical material of a chromosome (DNA + protein) is chromatin.

What is a gene?

The small part of DNA carrying hidden instructions in a language, in which information about making a protein is present, is called a gene. Each gene carries the information for making one protein.

Watson and Crick's model of DNA

According to Watson and Crick, DNA is a double helix made of two polynucleotide chains:

  • The outer part, i.e. the upright, is made of sugar and phosphate
  • The inner rungs are made of nitrogenous bases
  • Adenine always pairs with thymine
  • Cytosine always pairs with guanine
  • The bases are joined by hydrogen bonds
Part of DNAMake-up
UprightSugar and phosphate
RungNitrogenous bases: adenine and thymine, cytosine and guanine

Replication and gene expression

Copying of DNA is called replication. A gene expresses itself in two stages: transcription → mRNA is made from DNA; translation → the information in the mRNA is used to make a protein on the ribosome, which expresses the trait.

Multiple alleles: human blood groups

Some traits have more than two alternative forms of a gene; these are called multiple alleles. Its best example is the human ABO blood group system, which was discovered by Karl Landsteiner.

  • There are four blood groups: A, B, AB and O
  • Groups are formed on the basis of the antigens present on the red cells and the antibodies present in the blood serum
  • Mixing blood of the wrong group causes agglutination, which is dangerous
  • Blood of group O can be given to all groups, so group O is called the universal donor

options: The branch of biology that studies heredity and variation
The branch of biology that studies only plant nutrition
The transfer of genes from parents to offspring
The copying of DNA inside a cell
mcqs.q: What is genetics?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the branch of biology that studies heredity and variation. The notes define genetics in exactly these terms. Inheritance, not genetics, is the name given to the transfer of genes from parents to offspring.

options: The differences seen in organisms of a single species
The way parents transfer their genes to offspring
The joining of two chromatids at the centromere
The pairing of adenine with thymine
mcqs.q: What is meant by inheritance?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the way parents transfer their genes to offspring. The notes give this as the definition of inheritance. It is the process studied within the broader branch called genetics.

options: The outer upright part made of sugar and phosphate
The chemical material made of DNA and protein
The centre part where the two chromatids are joined
The small part of DNA that makes one protein
mcqs.q: What is the centromere of a chromosome?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the centre part where the two chromatids are joined. The notes state this definition for the centromere. A chromosome itself is described as a thread-like structure in each cell.

options: A nitrogenous base that pairs with guanine
A thread-like structure found in each cell
The hydrogen bond joining two bases
The chemical material of a chromosome, made of DNA and protein
mcqs.q: What is chromatin?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the chemical material of a chromosome, made of DNA and protein. The notes use the word chromatin for this material. It should not be confused with the chromosome structure itself.

options: The small part of DNA carrying instructions for making a protein
A complete chromosome with two chromatids
The blood serum containing antibodies
A group of cells that forms a blood group
mcqs.q: What is a gene?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the small part of DNA carrying instructions for making a protein. The notes say each gene carries the information for making one protein. This information is present in a coded, hidden form in the DNA.

options: A single chain made only of nitrogenous bases
A double helix made of two polynucleotide chains
A flat sheet made of sugar and protein
A ring made of four blood group antigens
mcqs.q: According to Watson and Crick, what is the structure of DNA?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is a double helix made of two polynucleotide chains. This is Watson and Crick's model of DNA as stated in the notes. The two chains form the uprights and rungs of the structure.

options: Only adenine and thymine
Only proteins and chromatin
Sugar and phosphate
Hydrogen bonds and ribosomes
mcqs.q: In DNA, what makes up the outer upright part of the double helix?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is sugar and phosphate. The notes state that the outer part, or upright, is made of sugar and phosphate. The inner rungs, by contrast, are made of nitrogenous bases.

options: Adenine with guanine, and cytosine with thymine
Adenine with cytosine, and thymine with guanine
Adenine with adenine, and cytosine with cytosine
Adenine with thymine, and cytosine with guanine
mcqs.q: How do the nitrogenous bases pair in DNA?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is adenine with thymine, and cytosine with guanine. The notes give these as the fixed base pairings in DNA. The bases in the inner rungs are joined by hydrogen bonds.

options: mRNA is made from DNA
A protein is made on the ribosome from mRNA
DNA is copied exactly into another DNA
Blood of the wrong group causes agglutination
mcqs.q: What happens during transcription in gene expression?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that mRNA is made from DNA. Transcription is the first of the two stages by which a gene expresses itself. In the second stage, translation, the mRNA information is used to make a protein.

options: Because it was discovered by Karl Landsteiner
Because blood of group O can be given to all groups
Because it has more than two alternative forms of a gene
Because it causes agglutination in all other groups
mcqs.q: Why is blood group O called the universal donor?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is because blood of group O can be given to all groups. The notes state this as the reason group O is called the universal donor. The ABO system itself was discovered by Karl Landsteiner.

lessons.title: Law of Segregation
lessons.notes_html:
Basic terms

  • Allele: different forms of a gene
  • Homozygous: both alleles alike, e.g. the same type of trait received from both parents
  • Heterozygous: both alleles different
  • Dominant allele: the one expressed in the heterozygous condition
  • Recessive allele: the one expressed only in the homozygous condition
  • Genotype: a trait's genetic makeup
  • Homologous: alike chromosomes
  • Heterologous: different chromosomes
TermRelation with dominant and recessive
Dominant traitAppears in the heterozygous condition, e.g. tall in Tt
Recessive traitAppears only in the homozygous condition, e.g. short in tt

Law of segregation

According to Mendel's law of segregation, the two factors, i.e. alleles, of each trait separate from each other when gametes are formed, and each gamete receives one factor.

Monohybrid cross

In a cross of a tall plant (TT) and a short plant (tt), all F1 plants are tall because they are heterozygous (Tt) and the dominant trait appears in them.

GametesTt
TTT tallTt tall
tTt talltt short

The result of the Tt × Tt cross is: TT, Tt, Tt, tt. So in F2 the ratio of tall to short plants is 3:1 — three parts tall because both TT and Tt have the dominant allele, and one part short.

Series: parents TT × tt → gametes T and t → F1 all Tt tall → cross of F1 among themselves → in F2, 3 tall and 1 short.

options: The genetic makeup of a trait
A pair of alike chromosomes
Different forms of a gene
A trait that appears only in the homozygous condition
mcqs.q: What is an allele?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is different forms of a gene. The notes define an allele in exactly this way under the basic terms. Genotype, by contrast, means a trait's genetic makeup.

options: When both alleles are different
When the trait appears in the heterozygous condition
When it receives gametes from two different parents
When both alleles are alike
mcqs.q: When is an organism described as homozygous for a trait?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is when both alleles are alike. The notes give the example of receiving the same type of trait from both parents. Heterozygous is the opposite condition, where both alleles are different.

options: The allele expressed in the heterozygous condition
The allele expressed only in the homozygous condition
An allele found only in gametes
An allele that separates during gamete formation
mcqs.q: What is a dominant allele?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the allele expressed in the heterozygous condition. The notes illustrate this with tallness appearing in Tt plants. A recessive allele, in contrast, is expressed only in the homozygous condition.

options: In both homozygous and heterozygous conditions
Only in the homozygous condition
Only when gametes are formed
Only in the F1 generation
mcqs.q: When is a recessive allele expressed?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is only in the homozygous condition. The notes give shortness in tt as the example of a recessive trait. In Tt plants the recessive allele is present but the dominant trait appears instead.

options: A pair of different chromosomes
The separation of alleles into gametes
A trait's genetic makeup
The visible tall or short appearance of a plant
mcqs.q: What does genotype mean?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is a trait's genetic makeup. The notes define genotype in these exact words. It refers to the alleles an organism carries for a trait, such as TT, Tt or tt.

options: Both alleles stay together in every gamete
Genes of different traits assort independently
All gametes receive both factors of a trait
The two alleles of each trait separate, and each gamete receives one factor
mcqs.q: According to Mendel's law of segregation, what happens when gametes are formed?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that the two alleles of each trait separate, and each gamete receives one factor. This is Mendel's law of segregation as stated in the notes. It explains why a Tt plant produces both T and t gametes.

options: All tall, because they are heterozygous (Tt) and the dominant trait appears
All short, because they are homozygous (tt)
Half tall and half short
Three tall for every one short
mcqs.q: In a cross between a tall plant (TT) and a short plant (tt), what are all the F1 plants like?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that all F1 plants are tall because they are heterozygous Tt and the dominant trait appears. The notes state this result for the TT cross with tt. The 3:1 ratio appears later, in the F2 generation.

options: All Tt
TT, Tt, Tt and tt
Only TT and tt
Only Tt and tt in equal numbers
mcqs.q: What genotypes result from a Tt x Tt cross?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is TT, Tt, Tt and tt. The Punnett square in the notes shows these four results from the Tt cross with Tt. This combination produces the familiar phenotypic ratio in F2.

mcqs.q: In the F2 generation of a monohybrid cross, what is the ratio of tall to short plants?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 3:1, three parts tall to one part short. The notes explain that both TT and Tt plants are tall because they carry the dominant allele. Only the tt plant is short.

options: Tall is recessive in Tt, and short is dominant in tt
Tall appears only in tt, and short appears in Tt
Both tall and short appear only in TT
Tall is the dominant trait in Tt, and short is the recessive trait in tt
mcqs.q: In the examples in the notes, which pairing matches a trait with its condition?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that tall is the dominant trait in Tt, and short is the recessive trait in tt. The notes give exactly these two examples for dominant and recessive traits. A dominant trait appears in the heterozygous condition, while a recessive trait appears only in the homozygous condition.

lessons.title: Law of Independent Assortment
lessons.notes_html:
What is the law of independent assortment?

This is Mendel's second law. According to this law, the genes of different traits are independent of each other in inheritance. When gametes are formed, the genes of one pair assort separately and independently of the genes of another pair.

Dihybrid cross

Mendel crossed two traits together: seed colour (yellow dominant, green recessive) and seed shape (round dominant, wrinkled recessive).

  • Parents (P): pure yellow round (RRYY) × pure green wrinkled (rryy)
  • First generation (F1): all plants were yellow and round, whose genotype is RrYy
  • Second generation (F2): when the F1 plants were crossed among themselves, four kinds of plants were produced

F2 ratio 9:3:3:1

Kind of plantNumber
Yellow and round9
Yellow and wrinkled3
Green and round3
Green and wrinkled1

From this ratio it was proved that the gene of colour and the gene of shape assort independently without affecting each other, so new combinations (yellow wrinkled and green round) also appeared in F2.

Types of gametes

A plant with genotype RrYy makes four kinds of gametes: RY, Ry, rY and ry. This is independent assortment: in each gamete, one gene from each pair goes independently.

options: The genes of different traits are independent of each other in inheritance
The two alleles of one trait separate when gametes are formed
A dominant allele is always expressed in the heterozygous condition
All F1 plants always show the recessive trait
mcqs.q: What is Mendel's law of independent assortment?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that the genes of different traits are independent of each other in inheritance. The notes present this as Mendel's second law. When gametes are formed, the genes of one pair assort separately from the genes of another pair.

options: Seed size and seed weight
Seed colour and seed shape
Plant height and flower colour
Seed colour and plant height
mcqs.q: In Mendel's dihybrid cross, which seed traits were crossed together?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is seed colour and seed shape. The notes say Mendel crossed these two traits together in the dihybrid cross. Yellow was dominant over green for colour, and round was dominant over wrinkled for shape.

options: Yellow and green are both dominant
Round is recessive and wrinkled is dominant
Yellow is dominant and green is recessive; round is dominant and wrinkled is recessive
Yellow is recessive and green is dominant; round is recessive and wrinkled is dominant
mcqs.q: Which traits are dominant and recessive in the dihybrid cross?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is yellow dominant and green recessive for colour, and round dominant and wrinkled recessive for shape. The notes state these relationships clearly. They determine the appearance of the F1 and F2 plants.

options: Pure yellow wrinkled and pure green round
Heterozygous yellow round and heterozygous yellow round
Pure green round and pure yellow wrinkled
Pure yellow round (RRYY) and pure green wrinkled (rryy)
mcqs.q: What were the parent plants in the dihybrid cross?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is pure yellow round RRYY crossed with pure green wrinkled rryy. The notes give these genotypes for the parent generation. Their offspring in F1 all had the genotype RrYy.

options: All yellow and round, with genotype RrYy
All green and wrinkled, with genotype rryy
Half yellow round and half green wrinkled
Nine yellow round for every one green wrinkled
mcqs.q: What were all the F1 plants like in the dihybrid cross?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that all F1 plants were yellow and round, with genotype RrYy. The notes state this result for the first generation. Both dominant traits appeared because each plant carried the dominant alleles.

mcqs.q: What is the F2 ratio in the dihybrid cross?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 9:3:3:1. The notes list nine yellow round, three yellow wrinkled, three green round and one green wrinkled plant. This ratio proved that the colour and shape genes assort independently.

options: 9 parts
1 part
3 parts
6 parts
mcqs.q: In the F2 generation, how many of the sixteen parts are yellow and wrinkled?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 3 parts. The notes' table for the 9:3:3:1 ratio gives three yellow and wrinkled plants. Yellow and wrinkled was one of the new combinations that appeared in F2.

options: That the two genes always stay together in gametes
That the recessive genes disappear in F2
That only the parent combinations can appear in F2
That the gene of colour and the gene of shape assort independently without affecting each other
mcqs.q: What did the F2 ratio prove about the genes for colour and shape?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that the gene of colour and the gene of shape assort independently without affecting each other. The notes state this conclusion from the 9:3:3:1 ratio. Because of it, new combinations such as yellow wrinkled and green round also appeared in F2.

options: Yellow wrinkled and green round
Yellow round and green wrinkled only
Green wrinkled and yellow round only
No new combinations appeared
mcqs.q: What new combinations appeared in the F2 generation?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is yellow wrinkled and green round. The notes name these as the new combinations in F2. They appeared because the colour and shape genes assorted independently of each other.

options: RR, YY, rr and yy
RY, Ry, rY and ry
Rr, Yy, RY and ry only as two kinds
Only RY and ry
mcqs.q: Which four kinds of gametes does a plant with genotype RrYy make?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is RY, Ry, rY and ry. The notes list these four kinds of gametes for a RrYy plant. This is independent assortment, because in each gamete one gene from each pair goes independently.

lessons.title: Variation and Evolution
lessons.notes_html:
What is variation?

The differences seen in the organisms of a single species are called variation. Variation can be passed to offspring through inheritance. According to Darwin, variations in organisms pass to the next generation through inheritance.

Darwin's theory of natural selection

  • Organisms produce more offspring than needed
  • Among them there is a struggle for existence
  • Variation exists in organisms
  • The fittest organisms survive
  • The surviving organisms pass their traits to offspring generation after generation
  • With the passage of time species change; this is evolution

Series: more offspring → struggle for existence → variation → survival of the fittest → transfer of traits → change in species. Organisms with variations suited to the environment survive and produce more offspring, so their traits increase from generation to generation.

Comparison of natural and artificial selection

Natural selectionArtificial selection
Takes place through natureIs done by humans
The fittest organisms surviveMan selects traits of his choice and breeds them

options: The transfer of genes from parents to offspring
The change of a whole species over a long time only
The differences seen in the organisms of a single species
The selection of traits by humans for breeding
mcqs.q: What is variation?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the differences seen in the organisms of a single species. The notes define variation in exactly these words. Such variation can be passed to offspring through inheritance.

options: Through artificial selection only
Through the struggle for existence
Through mixing of blood groups
Through inheritance
mcqs.q: How can variation be passed to offspring?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is through inheritance. The notes state that variation can be passed to offspring through inheritance. According to Darwin, variations in organisms pass to the next generation in this way.

options: More offspring than needed
Exactly as many offspring as can survive
Fewer offspring than needed
Offspring with no variation at all
mcqs.q: In Darwin's theory, what do organisms produce?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is more offspring than needed. This is the first point of Darwin's theory of natural selection in the notes. Because more offspring are produced than needed, a struggle for existence follows among them.

options: Artificial selection by humans
A struggle for existence among them
An immediate change of the whole species
The disappearance of all variation
mcqs.q: What follows from organisms producing more offspring than needed, according to Darwin's theory?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is a struggle for existence among them. The notes list this as the step after overproduction of offspring in Darwin's theory. Variation exists among the organisms taking part in this struggle.

options: All organisms equally
Only the organisms chosen by humans
The fittest organisms
Only the organisms with no variation
mcqs.q: In natural selection, which organisms survive?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the fittest organisms. The notes state that in Darwin's theory the fittest organisms survive the struggle for existence. The surviving organisms then pass their traits to offspring generation after generation.

options: They stop producing offspring
They lose their traits in the next generation
They are bred by humans for chosen traits
They pass their traits to offspring generation after generation
mcqs.q: What do the surviving organisms do, according to Darwin's theory?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that they pass their traits to offspring generation after generation. The notes include this step in the series for natural selection. Over time, this continued passing of traits leads to change in species.

options: The change of species with the passage of time
The differences seen within a single species at one moment
The breeding of animals by humans
The production of more offspring than needed
mcqs.q: What is evolution, as described in this lesson?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the change of species with the passage of time. The notes end the natural selection series with this outcome and call it evolution. It results from fitter traits being passed on generation after generation.

options: They fail in the struggle for existence
They survive and produce more offspring, so their traits increase from generation to generation
Their traits decrease from generation to generation
They can survive only if humans select them
mcqs.q: What happens to organisms with variations suited to the environment?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that they survive and produce more offspring, so their traits increase from generation to generation. The notes state this directly about variations suited to the environment. This increase is a key part of how natural selection works.

options: It is done by humans, and man selects traits of his choice
It takes place through gamete formation only
It takes place through nature, and the fittest organisms survive
It takes place in the laboratory, and all organisms survive
mcqs.q: How does natural selection take place, and what is its result?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that natural selection takes place through nature, and the fittest organisms survive. The comparison table in the notes gives both of these points for natural selection. Selection done by humans is artificial selection, not natural selection.

options: Selection that takes place through nature
The survival of the fittest organisms in nature
The struggle for existence among offspring
Selection done by humans, in which man selects traits of his choice and breeds them
mcqs.q: What is artificial selection?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is selection done by humans, in which man selects traits of his choice and breeds them. The notes give this description in the comparison with natural selection. Natural selection, by contrast, takes place through nature.

lessons.title: Ecosystem and Ecological Organization
lessons.notes_html:
What is the biosphere?

The layer around the earth that sustains life is called the biosphere. All organisms live in the biosphere.

Levels of ecological organization

  • Population: a group of organisms of one kind living in one area.
  • Community: the combined group of different organisms living in an area.
  • Ecosystem: the area where a community is in relation with the non-living environment; the combined system of a community and the non-living environment is the ecosystem.
  • Biome: a large biological region recognized by particular plants and a particular climate.
  • Biosphere: the combined big layer of all ecosystems.

Remember the order from small to big: population → community → ecosystem → biome → biosphere

Effect of light

Light is very essential for the ecosystem. Light is essential for photosynthesis; by it plants make food and the whole food chain of the ecosystem runs. Lack of light stops the growth of plants.

Biotic components of the ecosystem

The biotic components of an ecosystem are three:

ComponentWorkExample
ProducersMake their own food with the sun's energyPlants
ConsumersEat plants or other animalsPrimary, secondary and tertiary animals
DecomposersDecay dead organisms and return substances to the soilBacteria and fungi

Consumers are of three levels: the first level eats plants, the second level eats the first level, and the third level eats the second level.

options: The layer around the earth that sustains life
A group of organisms of one kind
A large region recognized by its climate
The non-living part of an ecosystem
mcqs.q: What is the biosphere?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the layer around the earth that sustains life. The notes state that all organisms live in the biosphere. It is not a single population or a single biome, but the layer in which life exists.

options: The combined group of different organisms in an area
A group of organisms of one kind living in one area
A community together with its non-living environment
The combined layer of all ecosystems
mcqs.q: What is a population in ecological organization?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is a group of organisms of one kind living in one area. A population is made of only one kind of organism. A combined group of different organisms is a community, not a population.

options: A group of organisms of one kind in one area
A large biological region with a particular climate
The combined group of different organisms living in an area
Organisms that decay dead bodies
mcqs.q: How is a community defined in the notes?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the combined group of different organisms living in an area. Unlike a population, which has only one kind, a community brings together different kinds of organisms. That difference is the key point in its definition.

options: Only the plants of an area
Only the non-living environment
Only one population in an area
A community combined with the non-living environment
mcqs.q: What makes up an ecosystem?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is a community combined with the non-living environment. The notes define an ecosystem as the area where a community is in relation with the non-living environment. Neither part alone makes an ecosystem.

options: Particular plants and a particular climate
One kind of animal and one kind of plant
Dead organisms and bacteria
Light and photosynthesis
mcqs.q: A biome is recognized by which two features?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is particular plants and a particular climate. The notes define a biome as a large biological region recognized by these two features. It is larger in scale than a single ecosystem.

options: Community, population, ecosystem, biome, biosphere

lessons.title: Energy Flow in the Ecosystem and Biogeochemical Cycles
lessons.notes_html:
What is a food chain?

The food material that passes from the producers among organisms as one eats another is called a food chain. A simple example: plant → herbivore → carnivore.

Trophic levels

Each step in a food chain is called a trophic level.

  • First trophic level: the producers (plants), because they make their own food from the sun's energy and feed all other organisms.
  • The second level is the primary consumer, the third level the secondary consumer, and so on.

Pyramid of numbers

The pyramid of numbers is the chart showing the number of organisms at each trophic level in an ecosystem. Generally the number is greater at the lower levels and smaller at the upper levels.

Biogeochemical cycles

The circulation of those elements of the ecosystem that are recycled through organisms is called a biogeochemical cycle. The nitrogen cycle and the carbon cycle are its examples.

Stages of the nitrogen cycle

StageWhat happens?
Nitrogen fixationAtmospheric nitrogen changes into compounds that plants can use; this takes place through lightning and nitrogen-fixing bacteria
NitrificationNitrogen compounds in organisms change into nitrates; ammonia → nitrates
Uptake by plantsPlants take up nitrates and make protein

The whole cycle runs like this: atmospheric nitrogen → fixation → ammonia → nitrification → nitrates → plants → animals → dead organisms → ammonia, and by denitrification nitrogen goes back into the air.

options: The chart showing numbers at each trophic level

mcqs.why: The correct answer is the food material that passes from the producers among organisms as one eats another. A food chain starts from the producers and moves as organisms eat one another. It is not a chart or a cycle of elements.

lessons.title: Interactions and Balance in the Ecosystem
lessons.notes_html:
Interactions among organisms

In an ecosystem, organisms are connected with each other in different ways. These interactions keep the balance of the ecosystem.

Competition

The cold war between organisms in an ecosystem for food and space is called competition. When food or space becomes less, competition takes place among the organisms wanting the same thing.

Symbiosis (mutual relationship)

The mutual relationship of two different organisms in which both benefit is called symbiosis. In its special form, neither can live without the other.

  • Example: in lichens, algae and fungi live together and both benefit each other.
  • Such a mutually beneficial relationship is also linked with mutualism.

Other interactions to remember

InteractionMeaning
CompetitionRivalry / cold war for food and space
SymbiosisBoth benefit, living without each other is difficult
PredationOne organism eats another
CommensalismOne benefits, the other neither benefits nor is harmed

Why is balance necessary?

If one kind of organism becomes too many or too few, the food chain breaks and the balance of the ecosystem is disturbed. Competition and mutual interactions help to keep numbers in balance.

lessons.title: Human Effects on the Environment
lessons.notes_html:
Human activities and the environment

Human activities have a big effect on the environment. The increase of gases, the spoiling of water and the ending of organisms are its results.

Greenhouse effect

The greenhouse effect is the trapping of the sun's heat on the earth by gases like carbon dioxide, which raises the earth's temperature. With rising temperature the climate changes.

Algal bloom

Algal bloom is the rapid growth of algae in water.

  • Algae grow rapidly and use up the water's oxygen.
  • Without oxygen, the water organisms die.
  • In this way the ecosystem is destroyed.

Remember the flow: rapid growth of algae → oxygen used up → water organisms die → ecosystem destroyed

Endangered species

Some organisms are in danger of ending. The endangered species found in Pakistan include:

  • Markhor
  • Snow leopard
  • Indus dolphin
  • Green turtle
  • Houbara bustard (talor)

Protecting these species is everyone's responsibility, because if one species ends, the food chain and balance are disturbed.

lessons.title: Pollution and Conservation of the Natural Environment
lessons.notes_html:
What is pollution?

Pollution is the addition of harmful substances to the environment. Pollution spoils air, water and soil — all three.

Air pollution

The increase in the amount of harmful gases in the air besides oxygen is called air pollution.

Type of pollutionHarmful effect
Air pollutionBreathing diseases, asthma, bronchitis, lung cancer, irritation of the eyes
Acid rain (a result of air pollution)Damage to crops
Damage to the ozone layerMore harmful rays of the sun reach us
Water pollutionWater organisms die, algal bloom takes place, drinking water is spoiled

Steps to stop water pollution

  • Factory waste water should be cleaned before releasing into rivers.
  • Garbage should not be thrown into water.
  • Less fertiliser and pesticide should be used in fields.
  • Water should be saved, not wasted.

Conservation of the natural environment

To save the environment, pollution must be reduced, endangered species must be protected, and water and air must be kept clean. Only in a clean environment do the balance of the ecosystem and human health remain.

lessons.title: Introduction to Biotechnology and the Fermentation Industry
lessons.notes_html:
What is biotechnology?

Biotechnology is the preparation of useful products and services for humans using biological systems, organisms or their parts.

Traditional biotechnology

Traditional biotechnology is the preparation of food and other products using organisms or their parts, such as making bread and curd by fermentation.

  • Biotechnology is an ancient technology: for thousands of years humans have made bread, curd, cheese and vinegar by fermentation.
  • Selecting better crops and animals by breeding is also ancient biotechnology.
  • The early biotechnologists were farmers, who made things like curd, bread and wine by fermentation.

Services of Louis Pasteur

  • Proved that fermentation is caused by living organisms (yeast).
  • Gave the method of pasteurization.
  • Laid the basis for vaccine preparation.

Industrial biotechnology and the fermenter

Large-scale preparation of alcohol and antibiotics through organisms is a special part of industrial biotechnology. The vessel used for large-scale production of bacteria is called a fermenter.

How does fermentation work?

Organisms produce energy (ATP) by breaking down food. Most organisms use oxygen to produce ATP. In fermentation glucose breaks down without oxygen:

Glucose → pyruvic acid → alcohol or lactic acid + a little energy

  • Organisms that carry out fermentation: yeast, some bacteria (such as Lactobacillus) and the muscles of animals in the absence of oxygen.
  • Factors affecting it: temperature, pH, presence of oxygen, amount of food (sugar) and type of organism.

Types of fermentation

TypeProduct
Alcoholic fermentationAlcohol + carbon dioxide; the released carbon dioxide makes the dough rise
Lactic acid fermentationLactic acid; lactic acid is formed from pyruvic acid
Acidic fermentationAcids like vinegar; lactic acid is formed from pyruvic acid

Products, advantages and disadvantages

Fermentation produces curd, cheese, bread, alcohol, vinegar, antibiotics and organic acids. Pakistani foods made through fermentation include curd, lassi, pickles, vinegar, leavened bread (naan, double roti) and cheese.

  • Lactobacillus: a bacterium which converts the sugar of milk (lactose) into lactic acid, so the milk sets into curd.
  • Advantages: food becomes tasty and easy to digest, keeps longer, and gains nutritional value.
  • Disadvantages: bad fermentation can spoil food and produce harmful substances.

lessons.title: Genetic Engineering
lessons.notes_html:
What is genetic engineering?

Artificially changing/modifying/rearranging DNA is called genetic engineering. By it, the gene of one organism is put into another organism and a new trait is produced.

Tools of recombinant DNA

Tool / enzymeWork
Restriction enzymeCuts DNA; bacteria naturally use it for their defence, they cut the DNA of viruses
Ligase enzymeRejoins the cut DNA
PlasmidExtra DNA used as a vector (carrier) for a gene

Steps of genetic engineering

Taking the desired gene → cutting DNA with a restriction enzyme → putting the gene into a plasmid → joining with ligase → putting the recombinant DNA into bacteria → production of the new product

Human Genome Project (HGP)

The study of the complete map of the human genome is the Human Genome Project (HGP). By it, the sequence and place of all human genes were found.

Recombinant products in the market

  • Insulin
  • Human growth hormone
  • Hepatitis B vaccine
  • Interferon

These products are obtained from recombinant DNA technology and are available in the market.

For their defence, by cutting the DNA of viruses
mcqs.q: How do bacteria naturally use restriction enzymes?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that bacteria use restriction enzymes for their defence, by cutting the DNA of viruses. This natural role is stated in the notes. In genetic engineering, the same cutting action is used as a tool of recombinant DNA technology.

options: It cuts DNA at a specific place
It acts as a carrier for a gene
It rejoins the cut DNA
It finds the sequence of all human genes
mcqs.q: What does the ligase enzyme do?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that ligase rejoins the cut DNA. After DNA is cut by a restriction enzyme and the desired gene is placed in a plasmid, ligase joins the pieces. Cutting DNA is the opposite job, done by the restriction enzyme.

options: An enzyme that cuts DNA
Extra DNA used as a vector (carrier) for a gene
A vessel for large-scale bacterial production
A protein obtained from microscopic organisms
mcqs.q: What is a plasmid in recombinant DNA technology?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that a plasmid is extra DNA used as a vector, or carrier, for a gene. The desired gene is put into a plasmid during the steps of genetic engineering. It is not an enzyme or a production vessel.

options: Taking the desired gene
Joining DNA with ligase
Putting recombinant DNA into bacteria
Production of the new product
mcqs.q: What is the first step of genetic engineering listed in the notes?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is taking the desired gene. The steps then continue with cutting DNA with a restriction enzyme, putting the gene into a plasmid and joining with ligase. Production of the new product comes only at the end of the sequence.

options: The DNA is cut again by ligase
The human genome is mapped
The plasmid is removed from the bacteria
Production of the new product takes place
mcqs.q: After the recombinant DNA is put into bacteria, what happens in the final step?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that production of the new product takes place. This is the last step in the sequence given in the notes, following the putting of recombinant DNA into bacteria. All the earlier cutting and joining steps lead to this production.

options: The production of protein from microscopic organisms
The large-scale preparation of alcohol and antibiotics
The study of the complete map of the human genome, by which the sequence and place of all human genes were found
The method of pasteurization given by Pasteur
mcqs.q: What is the Human Genome Project (HGP)?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that the Human Genome Project is the study of the complete map of the human genome. By it, the sequence and place of all human genes were found. It is a genome-mapping project, not a fermentation or protein-production process.

options: Curd
Insulin
Lassi
Vinegar
mcqs.q: Which of the following is a recombinant product available in the market?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is insulin. The notes list insulin, human growth hormone, hepatitis B vaccine and interferon as products obtained from recombinant DNA technology and available in the market. Curd, lassi and vinegar are fermentation products instead.

lessons.title: Single Cell Protein and Its Uses
lessons.notes_html:
What is single cell protein (SCP)?

Single cell protein is the protein obtained from the cells of microscopic organisms. This term was given in 1966 by Professor C. C. Wilson of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

What does SCP contain?

  • 60 to 80 percent of the dry weight of the cells is protein
  • It also contains nucleic acids, fats (lipids), minerals and vitamins
  • Some kinds have a higher amount of amino acids

Which organisms and which food (substrate)?

ThingExamples
OrganismsBacteria, yeast, fungi, algae
Carbon substratesn-alkanes, alcohol products, sulphite, molasses, whey (milk water)
Place of productionGrown inside a fermenter on a large scale

Uses and advantages

  • Single cell protein is included in the food of very many animals; it is especially used as animal food and as a nutritional supplement
  • Some waste substances can be made useful by fermentation, e.g. products can be made using grass, wood or straw
  • Leftover waste, leftover alcohol and human and animal waste can also be used as substrate, which also reduces the waste problem

options: The protein obtained from the cells of microscopic organisms
The protein formed when milk sets into curd
A gene carrier used in genetic engineering
An acid produced during fermentation of glucose
mcqs.q: What is single cell protein (SCP)?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the protein obtained from the cells of microscopic organisms. This is the definition of single cell protein given in the notes. It is grown on a large scale inside a fermenter.

options: Louis Pasteur, in the time of pasteurization
Professor C. C. Wilson, in 1966, at a food factory
Professor C. C. Wilson, before fermentation was understood
Professor C. C. Wilson of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, in 1966
mcqs.q: Who gave the term single cell protein, and when?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is Professor Wilson of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, in 1966. The notes give both the year and the institute with his name. Louis Pasteur is linked with fermentation and pasteurization, not with this term.

options: 10 to 20 percent
60 to 80 percent
30 to 40 percent
90 to 100 percent
mcqs.q: How much of the dry weight of SCP cells is protein?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 60 to 80 percent of the dry weight of the cells is protein. This high protein content is stated in the notes. SCP also contains nucleic acids, fats (lipids), minerals and vitamins.

options: Only water and lactose

Nucleic acids, fats (lipids), minerals and vitamins
Only restriction enzymes and ligase
mcqs.q: Besides protein, what else does single cell protein contain?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is nucleic acids, fats (lipids), minerals and vitamins. The notes list these components along with protein in SCP. Some kinds of SCP also have a higher amount of amino acids.

options: Bacteria, yeast, fungi and algae
Only animals and plants
Only viruses and bacteria
Only human and animal cells
mcqs.q: Which organisms are used to produce single cell protein?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is bacteria, yeast, fungi and algae. These are the organisms listed in the notes for SCP production. They are microscopic organisms grown inside a fermenter on a large scale.

options: Insulin
Interferon
Pyruvic acid
Molasses
mcqs.q: Which of the following is a carbon substrate for SCP production?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is molasses. The notes list n-alkanes, alcohol products, sulphite, molasses and whey (milk water) as carbon substrates. Insulin and interferon are recombinant products, not substrates for SCP.

options: In open fields
Inside a fermenter
Inside a plasmid
In the muscles of animals
mcqs.q: Where is single cell protein produced on a large scale?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is inside a fermenter. The notes state that SCP organisms are grown inside a fermenter on a large scale. A plasmid is a gene carrier in genetic engineering, not a place of production.

options: A vaccine against hepatitis B
A method of pasteurization
Animal food and a nutritional supplement
A vector for transferring genes
mcqs.q: What is single cell protein especially used as?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is animal food and a nutritional supplement. The notes say SCP is included in the food of very many animals and is especially used in these two ways. It is a protein source, not a vaccine or a gene vector.

options: Grass, wood or straw
Glass, plastic or metal
Rocks, sand or minerals
Restriction enzymes or plasmids
mcqs.q: Which waste materials can be used to make products by fermentation, according to the notes?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is grass, wood or straw. The notes say some waste substances can be made useful by fermentation, and products can be made using grass, wood or straw. This turns waste material into something useful.

mcqs.why: The correct answer is that it reduces the waste problem. The notes state that leftover waste, leftover alcohol and human and animal waste can also be used as substrate, which also reduces the waste problem. SCP production therefore gives a double benefit.

lessons.title: Introduction to Pharmacology and Medicines for Diseases
lessons.notes_html:
Pharmacology and sources of medicines

Medicines are obtained from different natural sources. Medicines from natural sources are obtained by extracting and purifying substances from plants, animals and microorganisms.

SourceParts / examples
PlantsLeaves, bark, roots; the medicine for Rheumatoid Arthritis (aspirin-like drug) is obtained from plants
AnimalsGlands, liver; insulin (from the pancreas of cow/pig), heparin (from the liver), cod liver oil (from fish liver)
MicroorganismsMedicines are extracted and purified from fungi and bacteria
MineralsMinerals are also a source of medicines

Founder of antiseptic

Joseph Lister is considered the founder of antiseptic. With antiseptics, germs in wounds are killed and infection is prevented.

Names to remember

  • Lister — founder of antiseptic
  • Alexander Fleming, Edward Jenner and Louis Pasteur are other famous names, but the founder of antiseptic is Lister.

options: By mixing minerals in a laboratory only
By extracting and purifying substances from plants, animals and microorganisms
By collecting them directly without any processing
By making them only from fungi and bacteria
mcqs.q: How are medicines from natural sources obtained according to the notes?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is by extracting and purifying substances from plants, animals and microorganisms. The notes state that medicines from natural sources are obtained in this way. This process separates the useful substances in a purified form.

Only roots and stems
Leaves, bark and roots
Only leaves and fruits
mcqs.q: Which plant parts are mentioned in the notes as sources of medicines?

options: Plants

mcqs.why: The correct answer is plants. The notes state that the medicine for Rheumatoid Arthritis, the aspirin-like drug, is obtained from plants. It is not listed under animals, minerals or microorganisms.

options: Fish liver
Plant leaves
Fungi

mcqs.q: Insulin is obtained from which source as stated in the notes?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the pancreas of cow/pig. The notes give insulin as an animal-source medicine obtained from the pancreas of cow or pig. Fish liver and plant leaves are mentioned for different medicines.

options: Pancreas of cow/pig
Liver

mcqs.q: Medicines from microorganisms are extracted and purified from what?

mcqs.q: Which of the following is also listed in the notes as a source of medicines?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is minerals. The notes clearly state that minerals are also a source of medicines, in addition to plants, animals and microorganisms. Sunlight, air and plastics are not listed as sources.

lessons.title: Addictive Drugs
lessons.notes_html:
Addictive drugs

Some drugs have such an effect on the brain and body that a person becomes addicted to them. Such a habit is called drug addiction and it is very dangerous.

Type of drugEffect
SedativesSlow down brain activity and bring sleep
HallucinogensEffects like seeing imaginary things and sudden happiness
NarcoticsOne type of addictive drugs
MarijuanaCounted among addictive substances

Why is the use of sedatives increasing?

  • Stress (tension) has increased.
  • Anxiety has increased.
  • Complaints of sleeplessness have increased.
  • People rely on them for rest and sleep and then become addicted to them.

Why is drug addiction dangerous?

  • Addiction damages the brain and the body.
  • Health is destroyed.
  • Problems are created in the family and society.
  • A person becomes a slave of the drug.

Therefore addiction should be avoided and such medicines should not be used without a doctor's advice.

options: The use of a medicine on a doctor's advice
The slowing down of brain activity
The habit formed when a person becomes addicted to certain drugs because of their effect on the brain and body
Seeing imaginary things and feeling sudden happiness
mcqs.q: What is called drug addiction in the notes?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the habit formed when a person becomes addicted to certain drugs because of their effect on the brain and body. The notes call this habit drug addiction and describe it as very dangerous. It is not the normal use of medicine on a doctor's advice.

options: They slow down brain activity and bring sleep
They make a person see imaginary things
They kill germs in wounds and prevent infection
They stop the growth of bacteria
mcqs.q: What is the effect of sedatives as described in the notes?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that sedatives slow down brain activity and bring sleep. The notes give this as the specific effect of sedatives. Seeing imaginary things is linked with hallucinogens, not with sedatives.

options: Sleeplessness and anxiety only
Destruction of useful bacteria
Allergy and diarrhoea
Seeing imaginary things and sudden happiness
mcqs.q: Hallucinogens produce effects such as what according to the notes?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is seeing imaginary things and sudden happiness. The notes describe these as the effects of hallucinogens. Allergy and diarrhoea are harms linked with misuse of antibiotics, not with hallucinogens.

options: They are a source of medicines obtained from plants

mcqs.why: The correct answer is that narcotics are one type of addictive drugs. The notes list narcotics in the table of addictive drugs. Weakened or dead germs are the contents described for a vaccine, not for narcotics.

options: Antibiotics
Vaccines
Addictive substances
Antiseptics

mcqs.why: The correct answer is addictive substances. The notes clearly count marijuana among addictive substances. It is not described as an antibiotic, a vaccine or an antiseptic in the notes.

options: Because minerals have become a source of medicines
Because bacteria have developed resistance
Because germs in wounds need to be killed
Because stress, anxiety and complaints of sleeplessness have increased
mcqs.q: According to the notes, why is the use of sedatives increasing?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that stress, anxiety and complaints of sleeplessness have increased. The notes give all three as reasons for the increasing use of sedatives. Bacterial resistance and wound germs belong to other topics in the chapter.

options: They rely on them for rest and sleep and then become addicted to them
They take them by injection or drops before disease
They recognise them and make antibodies against them
They make enzymes that break them down
mcqs.q: How do people become addicted to sedatives according to the notes?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that people rely on sedatives for rest and sleep and then become addicted to them. The notes explain this dependence as the path to addiction. Making enzymes that break down a drug is part of how bacteria develop antibiotic resistance.

options: It develops immunity in the body before disease

mcqs.q: What damage does drug addiction cause as stated in the notes?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that addiction damages the brain and the body and destroys health. The notes list these harms to show why drug addiction is very dangerous. Antibodies and memory cells are made after vaccination, not because of addiction.

mcqs.why: The correct answer is that addiction creates problems in the family and society and makes a person a slave of the drug. The notes mention both these effects of addiction. Spreading resistance is an effect linked with bacteria, not with drug addiction.

mcqs.q: What advice is given in the notes about addictive medicines?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that addiction should be avoided and such medicines should not be used without a doctor's advice. The notes give this advice because addiction damages the brain, the body and health. Using them freely for rest and sleep leads to addiction.

lessons.title: Antibiotics and Vaccines
lessons.notes_html:
Antibiotics

Antibiotics are medicines that work against bacteria.

  • Bacteriostatic: things that stop the growth of bacteria but do not kill them.
  • Bactericidal: the word connected with the property of killing bacteria.

Why don't antibiotics work against viruses?

Antibiotics act on the walls and processes of bacteria; viruses lack those structures and live inside cells, so antibiotics do not affect them.

Misuse of antibiotics and its harm

  • Destruction of useful bacteria
  • Allergy
  • Diarrhoea
  • Antibiotic resistance — the biggest result of misuse

How do bacteria develop resistance?

A resistant trait is produced by mutation → bacteria make enzymes that break down the antibiotic, pump it out, or change their target → resistant bacteria survive and multiply, and resistance spreads to other bacteria.

Vaccine and vaccination

A vaccine is given before disease so that immunity develops in the body.

  • In vaccination the vaccine is given into the body by injection or drops.
  • It contains weakened or dead germs which do not cause disease.
  • The body recognises them and makes antibodies and memory cells.
  • When the real germs arrive, the body destroys them at once.

Flow: vaccine (weakened/dead germs) → recognition by the body → antibodies + memory cells → on arrival of real germs, immediate destruction → protection from disease

ThingWhen / work
VaccineBefore disease, for immunity
AntibioticIn bacterial disease, ineffective against viruses
BacteriostaticStops the growth of bacteria, does not kill

options: Bacteria
Viruses only
Fungi only
All germs including viruses
mcqs.q: Antibiotics are medicines that work against what?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is bacteria. The notes define antibiotics as medicines that work against bacteria. They are specifically described as ineffective against viruses, so they do not work against all germs.

options: Killing bacteria completely
Making antibodies and memory cells
Developing antibiotic resistance in bacteria
Stopping the growth of bacteria but not killing them
mcqs.q: What does bacteriostatic mean according to the notes?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is stopping the growth of bacteria but not killing them. The notes define bacteriostatic in exactly this way. Killing bacteria is the property connected with the word bactericidal, not bacteriostatic.

options: Stopping bacterial growth only
Killing bacteria
Living inside cells
Preventing disease before it occurs
mcqs.q: The word bactericidal is connected with which property?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is killing bacteria. The notes connect the word bactericidal with the property of killing bacteria. This is different from bacteriostatic, which only stops bacterial growth without killing.

options: Because viruses make memory cells in the body
Because viruses cause allergy and diarrhoea
Because viruses lack the walls and processes of bacteria that antibiotics act on and live inside cells
Because bacteria pump antibiotics out of the cell
mcqs.q: Why do antibiotics not work against viruses according to the notes?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that viruses lack the walls and processes of bacteria that antibiotics act on and live inside cells. The notes give this as the reason antibiotics do not affect viruses. Pumping out an antibiotic is a method used by resistant bacteria.

options: Destruction of useful bacteria
Allergy
Antibiotic resistance
Diarrhoea
mcqs.q: Which result of misuse of antibiotics is described as the biggest result in the notes?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is antibiotic resistance. The notes call antibiotic resistance the biggest result of misuse of antibiotics. Destruction of useful bacteria, allergy and diarrhoea are also listed as harms of misuse, but resistance is singled out as the biggest.

options: They recognise it and make antibodies and memory cells
They make enzymes that break down the antibiotic, pump it out, or change their target
They kill germs in wounds and prevent infection
They slow down brain activity and bring sleep
mcqs.q: How do bacteria deal with an antibiotic after a resistant trait is produced by mutation?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that bacteria make enzymes that break down the antibiotic, pump it out, or change their target. The notes describe these three actions after a resistant trait is produced by mutation. Antibodies and memory cells are made by the human body after vaccination.

options: They are destroyed at once when real germs arrive
They develop immunity before disease
They stop growing but never multiply
They survive and multiply, and resistance spreads to other bacteria
mcqs.q: What happens to resistant bacteria and their resistance according to the notes?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that resistant bacteria survive and multiply, and resistance spreads to other bacteria. The notes give this as the final step in how bacteria develop resistance. It follows the production of a resistant trait by mutation.

options: Before disease, so that immunity develops in the body
During bacterial disease, to kill bacteria directly
After disease, to stop the growth of bacteria
Only when a virus lives inside a cell
mcqs.q: When is a vaccine given and for what purpose according to the notes?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is before disease, so that immunity develops in the body. The notes clearly state this timing and purpose for a vaccine. An antibiotic, not a vaccine, is used in bacterial disease.

options: Strong live germs that cause disease, given by mouth only
Antibiotics, given by injection only
Weakened or dead germs which do not cause disease, given by injection or drops
Useful bacteria, given by drops only
mcqs.q: What does a vaccine contain and how is it given into the body?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is weakened or dead germs which do not cause disease, given by injection or drops. The notes state both the contents of a vaccine and the two ways it is given. These germs are recognised by the body without causing the disease.

options: Enzymes that break down antibiotics, and the germs are pumped out
Antibodies and memory cells, and the body destroys the real germs at once
A sedative effect, and the body goes to sleep
Resistance that spreads to other bacteria
mcqs.q: What does the body make after it recognises the germs in a vaccine, and what happens when real germs arrive?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is antibodies and memory cells, and the body destroys the real germs at once when they arrive. The notes describe this sequence as how vaccination gives protection from disease. Resistance spreading to bacteria is a separate process linked with antibiotic misuse.
